title: Cultural Humility
subtitle: Learning what something means to the person, examining your own reading, and minding the influence your role carries
summary: Knowing a service well does not mean knowing what it means to every person who uses it. This course builds cultural humility as the readings define it: ongoing self-examination, attention to unequal influence, and partnership that gives people a real choice. You practice separating what someone said from the meaning you added, asking questions with a purpose, hearing a correction without defending yourself, and carrying what you learn into the structured tools and real responsibilities of DHS work. A workplace simulation lets you try these moves when a member of the public says a DHS appointment letter left her lost outside the building.
objectives: Explain cultural humility as an ongoing practice of self-examination, attention to unequal influence and partnership, and say what it is not.
Separate what a person actually said or did from the meaning your own learned experience added to it.
Ask a question with a clear purpose that lets the person's answer change your interpretation, without making personal disclosure the price of help.
Respond to a correction by naming the specific inference you got wrong, without defending your intention or asking for reassurance.
Use structured tools and real responsibilities alongside humility, and describe what you learned, what you did and what is still unknown as different things.

narrator.voice_notes: Warm, steady colleague who has done this work and still gets it wrong sometimes. Unhurried pace, short sentences, plain words. Curious rather than certain. Quoted dialogue in a slightly different, conversational tone. Never lecturing, never grading. Confirm pronunciation of Tervalon, Murray-García and DeBlaere before recording.

segments.title: Welcome and why it matters

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Cultural Humility. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, facing the viewer with a warm, open expression, hands loosely clasped.
on_screen: Cultural Humility
Learning what something means to the person, and examining your own interpretation
scenes.narration: Welcome. You already know a lot about your work. You know the programs, the forms, the steps and the people you work beside. That knowledge matters, and nothing in this course asks you to set it aside. This course is about the moment when your knowledge meets another person's experience, and the two do not quite match. Knowing a service well does not mean knowing what it means to every person who uses it. Cultural humility helps you keep that difference in view. It means learning what something means to the person in front of you. It means looking honestly at the interpretation you bring. And it means paying attention to the influence your public-service role carries. You will look at what that involves, try a few practices, and then step into a workplace situation where your choices shape what happens next.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Correct and still hard to use. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, turned slightly toward the points, one hand raised toward the second line.
on_screen: The address is correct.
The entrance is still hard to find.
Both accounts answer different questions.
scenes.narration: Here is a small example that shows up in several of the readings behind this course. Staff send a letter with the correct building address. A person arrives and walks around the building, unable to tell which door is the public entrance. Staff check the address. It is right. The person's experience is also real. Both accounts matter, and they answer different questions. The address answers where the building is. The person's account answers whether someone new can actually get in. When the reply is, “The directions are complete,” the person's knowledge gets set aside. Nothing dramatic happened. No one meant harm. Yet if unclear routes are always called complete, insiders get in more easily. People meeting the process for the first time do not. Small exchanges like this one, repeated, shape who a public service works for.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Two sides of humility. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, gesturing first toward one point, then toward the other.
on_screen: Inward: an accurate view of yourself, including your limits
Outward: focus on the other person, with curiosity
scenes.narration: Counseling psychologist Joshua Hook and three colleagues have studied humility in helping relationships. They describe two sides. The inward side is an accurate view of yourself, including your limits. The outward side is focusing on the other person with curiosity. In their research, when clients rated their therapist as culturally humble, that rating predicted a stronger working relationship and better outcomes. Two cautions come with that finding. Most of the evidence comes from therapy and relies on what clients report about their experience. Using it in case management, benefits work or policy work takes some adaptation. The reading also notes a criticism some people raise: a focus on personal humility can play down inequities built into systems. It works best paired with efforts at the system level. Keep both points in mind as you go.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: The path ahead. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, half-turned toward the list, one hand open toward it.
on_screen: What it is, and your own assumptions
Curiosity, listening and repair
Your work, then a workplace simulation
scenes.narration: Here is the path ahead. First, what cultural humility is and is not, as the readings define it. Then you turn toward your own assumptions, the meanings you add without noticing. Next come practices for curiosity, listening and respect. After that, what to do when it goes wrong, because sometimes it will. Then you look at how humility fits the structured tools and real duties in DHS work. Each part ends with a few questions to think over, alone or with a colleague you trust. Before you go on, bring one real situation from your own work to mind. A conversation, a letter, a meeting. Keep that question within easy reach as you continue. Let it travel with you through each of the remaining segments.

check.prompt: A person says the appointment letter did not help them find the public entrance. Staff confirm the address is correct. Which reading fits the example best?

options.text: The address answers where the building is, and the person's account answers whether someone new can get in. Both belong in the response.

feedback.text: You kept both accounts in view. The checked address stays useful, and the person's experience points to something the letter does not yet say. Build on that by asking which part of the route was unclear.
Next time you hear a concern like this, try: “The address is right, so tell me where along the way it got confusing.”

options.text: Staff checked the address against the official listing and it is correct, so the letter is accurate and the concern can be closed with a polite reply.

feedback.text: The address check answers where the building is. The concern is about which door to use. A stronger response keeps the accurate fact and still asks about the gap the person found.
From outside the building, a correct address can still leave you walking past doors that all look alike. The person knows something staff cannot see from inside.

options.text: If one person could not find the door, many others likely could not either, so the whole letter should be rewritten before it goes to anyone else.

feedback.text: Wanting to fix it fully is a caring reaction. One account shows a real gap worth examining; it does not yet show what every visitor needs. Start with the specific difficulty.
What would you want to learn before deciding how big the change should be?

reflection: Think of a process you know well. What might a person meeting it for the first time need that you no longer notice?
When has someone's account of your work told you something you could not have seen from your side?
Where in your work does a correct answer sometimes stand in for a usable one?

segments.title: What cultural humility is and is not

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Three commitments. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, standing upright and speaking to the viewer.
on_screen: Ongoing self-examination
Attention to unequal power
Respectful partnership
scenes.narration: The idea of cultural humility comes from a 1998 paper by Tervalon and Murray-Garcia, written for medical education. They described three commitments. First, lifelong self-examination and self-critique: continuing to look at how your own learned expectations shape what you see. Second, attention to power: noticing the imbalance between the professional and the person being served. Third, partnership that benefits both sides and does not decide things for people. Their setting was doctors and patients. Your setting is different, and the readings behind this course are careful about that. They borrow the three ideas, not the clinical procedures. Self-examination, power and partnership can guide how you answer a call, write a notice, run a meeting or review a policy. They do not turn into a legal rule or a step-by-step procedure for every DHS program.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Two friends and one offer. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse, with locs (C2) stands full length, relaxed, with a small friendly smile, as the second friend, who declined the offer.
on_screen: What happened: the second friend declined help packing.
What the first friend heard: distance.
What the second friend said: nothing about the friendship.
scenes.narration: One reading uses a story about two friends getting ready for a move. The first friend learned that accepting practical help shows trust and shared care. The second friend learned that making arrangements yourself shows responsibility and avoids imposing on others. When the second friend declines an offer to help pack, the first friend's first thought is, “My friend does not value our friendship.” The second friend has not said that. Neither meaning needs to be tied to a nationality, a family type or a group. The second friend can value the friendship and still decline this one offer. Knowing their own way of caring cannot tell the first friend what the second friend intended. A better next step is a question: “Would help feel useful, or would you rather make the arrangements yourself?” That is the heart of the practice. You keep your first reading open long enough for the other person's meaning to reach you.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: What it is not. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, one hand raised slightly, counting the points off.
on_screen: Not just modesty
Not giving up your expertise
Not agreeing to everything or setting aside real duties
scenes.narration: Cultural humility is easy to misread, so it helps to say what it is not. It is not just being modest, or saying you do not know everything. It asks you to look at how your expectations affect an exchange, and whether another person's view can actually change your response. It is not giving up your expertise. A community brief may explain useful history. Your role may carry knowledge people need. Neither one gives you complete knowledge of a person's priorities. It is not agreeing to every request. You can understand what someone is asking, explain a real limit, and look for an alternative, all without promising something you cannot provide. And it does not set aside your real duties. Humility improves the basis for your response. It does not replace decisions that belong to the person or area responsible for them.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Knowledge and meaning. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the royal blue blouse (C5) stands full length, holding a worn serving bowl in both hands, as the bowl's owner.
on_screen: Knowledge: what the object was made for
The person's meaning: what it means to them now
scenes.narration: You may have heard cultural humility set against cultural competence, as if one knows everything and the other knows nothing. The readings push back on that. The 1998 authors challenged the idea of competence as finished mastery. Hook and his colleagues go further and call mastering facts about groups a goal no one can reach. Yet the National Center for Cultural Competence describes its own framework as developmental, including self-assessment and adaptation as well as knowledge. So the two need not be rivals. One reading shows how they fit. A person researches an old bowl that a friend inherited. The researcher learns its period, its materials and how such bowls were often used. That is useful. Then the researcher assumes its owner should keep it on a shelf, untouched. The owner explains that using it carefully every day keeps a loved person present. History and the owner's meaning answer different questions. The researcher needs both.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A stance, not a credential. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, facing the viewer, hands at rest.
on_screen: A stance, not a credential
Knowledge informs the question. It does not answer for the person.
scenes.narration: Hook and his colleagues put it simply: cultural humility is a stance, not a credential. You do not finish it. Finishing this course will not mean you understand everyone's culture, and no label like humble or competent tells you what someone actually understood or did. A specific account says far more. The researcher learned the bowl's history and reconsidered an assumption about the bowl's owner. That leaves room for the next question. The same is true of you. Each conversation can clarify one interpretation and change one response. That is real progress. It is not mastery, and it does not need to be. Hold on to one line from the readings as you go: knowledge informs the question, it does not answer for the individual. Your experience helps you ask better questions. The person still holds the answer about their own life.

check.prompt: Which description of cultural humility matches the readings?

options.text: An ongoing practice: examining your own interpretations, noticing unequal influence and working in partnership, while still using what you know.

feedback.text: You held all three ideas together and kept knowledge in the picture. Extend it by noticing which of the three you lean on least in your own work.

options.text: Being honest that you cannot know everything about other cultures, and saying so openly, so people know you are not claiming to be an expert on their lives.

feedback.text: Admitting limits is a start. The readings ask for more: examining how your expectations shape the exchange, and letting the other person's account actually change your response.

options.text: Building solid knowledge of each cultural group's customs and values, so you can anticipate what the people you serve will want before they have to explain.

feedback.text: Many trainings have taught exactly this, so it is a common picture. The readings call mastery of group facts unreachable. Facts can sharpen your question; they cannot answer for one person.

options.text: Setting your own expertise aside so the person's view leads, and agreeing to what people ask, because they know their own lives best.

feedback.text: A person relying on you needs your knowledge and honest limits. Agreeing to everything can leave them with promises no one can keep.

reflection: Which of the three commitments, self-examination, attention to power or partnership, comes most easily to you? Which takes more effort?
Think of something you know well about a community or a program. What question about one person does that knowledge still leave open?
Where have you seen humility mistaken for agreeing to everything?

segments.title: Looking at your own assumptions

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Observation or added reason. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, turned slightly toward the two sentences, one hand open.
on_screen: Observation: “The form was not returned.”
Added reason: “The person is not interested.”
scenes.narration: Compare two sentences. “The form was not returned.” That is an observation. “The person is not interested.” That adds a reason. An unfinished step can have many explanations. The person may have misunderstood. There may be a practical barrier. They may disagree, or their plans may have changed, or something else entirely is going on. A sound judgment keeps three things apart: the facts, the possible explanations, and the information you would need to choose a response. This is not about doubting everything. It is about noticing the moment your mind supplies a reason, and asking whether the person supplied it or you did.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: What was asked, what was added. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the navy polo (C4) stands full length, holding a printed sheet with two appointment options, as the staff member at the counter.
on_screen: The person asked: to compare options with someone she trusts.
The staff member added: she is reluctant to decide.
scenes.narration: A public-service version comes from the readings. A staff member has prepared a clear explanation of two appointment options. The person he is serving listens and asks, “Can I compare the arrangements with someone I trust before I choose?” The staff member has a complete answer ready, and takes the question as reluctance to decide. She has not said that. She asked about chosen advice. He added the motive. If he believes she is reluctant, his next move is pressure to decide now. If he keeps her actual words in front of him, his next move is a question: which part would you like to compare? Then he explains what the appointment process actually allows. Same person, same moment. The added meaning changes the whole response.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Learned meanings. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, speaking to the viewer, hands loosely together.
on_screen: A settled answer can show respect for someone's time.
A shared question can show respect for a shared result.
Neither is a rule for a group.
scenes.narration: Why did reluctance feel like the natural reading? The story goes further. The staff member remembers a school debate group where you prepared a complete position before inviting questions. Doing the work first showed respect for the audience. A colleague of his learned something different in a community orchestra. Members asked each other what a passage meant before deciding how to play it. An open question showed responsibility for a shared result. Both are ways of acting responsibly. Then the person he is serving adds, “I want to ask my friend about travel time. I still want to tell you which route I choose.” Now the staff member can see that talking it through may prepare her own decision rather than delay it. The colleague's account belongs to that colleague. It is not a rule for a nationality, a family or all musicians. Learned meanings come from experience within its setting. They are not predicted from someone's identity.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Three paths after a reaction. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, standing calmly, speaking gently to the viewer.
on_screen: Self-blame: “My value is a flaw.”
Self-defense: “My value is right, so they should accept it.”
Self-examination: “Does my value fit this moment?”
scenes.narration: Looking at your own assumptions can feel uncomfortable, so it helps to know what this is not. Go back to the two friends. The first friend heard the second friend's refusal as distance, and remembers neighbors sharing tasks during a hard time. Accepting help meant belonging. That memory explains the reaction. It does not establish what the second friend owes. The first friend has three paths. Self-blame says the value is foolish and tries to suppress it. That swaps one rigid judgment for another. Self-defense lists reasons why help is good and concludes the second friend should accept it. That leaves the mistaken inference untouched. Self-examination notices the link between help and belonging, then asks whether it fits this refusal. A value is not an entitlement. The first friend can keep caring about mutual help and still change how it is offered. Self-critique examines your reasoning. It does not ask for shame, and it does not ask you to tell anyone your history.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A request, not a reason. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, turned toward the points, one hand lightly raised.
on_screen: Valuing family is not the same as wanting family in every conversation.
Ask what participation means now.
scenes.narration: Assumptions also hide inside good intentions. In one reading, staff invite family to a planning conversation because family involvement is usually helpful. The person asks to speak privately. The request tells you something real: the arrangement the person wants. It does not tell you why, and you do not need to fill that gap with a cultural explanation. The person also does not owe you a cultural biography to justify asking. Someone can value family and still want to discuss one issue alone. A value is not a fixed instruction for every situation. Circumstances and preferences change. So ask about the present purpose, the chosen support and the arrangement the person wants, and let the answer shape what you offer.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Narrow the label. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, holding a small notepad and pen.
on_screen: “Quiet in the meeting” is narrower than “not committed.”
“Questioned the instruction” is narrower than “does not understand the service.”
scenes.narration: Here is a practice you can use anywhere. Take a label that comes easily. One reading offers three: declined help, quiet in the meeting, asked about the instruction. Notice how much narrower each one is than the label it tends to grow into. Quiet in the meeting is narrower than not committed. Asked about the instruction is narrower than does not understand the service. Write down what you actually observed. Name one assumption you could reconsider. Then write a question that could change it. Finally, trace what might happen if the wider label stayed. Would it end up in a note someone else reads? Would it mean fewer choices offered next time? You can do this in a minute, in your head, before you hit send. The point is to keep room for evidence that does not fit your first account.

check.prompt: A staff member has prepared two appointment options. The person he is serving asks to compare them with someone she trusts, and he hears reluctance. What should he examine first?

options.text: The difference between what she actually asked for, a chance to compare the options with someone she trusts, and the reluctance he added to it.

feedback.text: You put the actual request back at the center. From there he can ask what she wants to compare and explain what the process allows. Try spotting the same gap in your own next exchange.
When did you last hear a question as hesitation, and what did the person actually ask?

options.text: Which cultural or family background might explain her hesitation, so he can respond in a way that fits what people like her usually expect.

feedback.text: A group explanation predicts her meaning without her. Examining his own inference lets him respond to what she actually said.
She asked a practical question. Being explained by a group label could leave her feeling unheard as a person.

options.text: Whether his explanation of the two options was clear and complete enough, since a gap in what he said could be why she wants a second opinion.

feedback.text: Good preparation can make an answer feel complete. Being prepared is valuable. It still cannot tell him which question remains open for her.
After explaining, try asking, “Which part would you like to look at more closely?”

reflection: Pick one label you used about someone at work this month. What did you actually observe?
What is a value you learned early that makes certain behavior feel respectful to you? Where might it not fit someone else?
Where could a first impression of yours travel after the conversation ends, such as a note, an assignment or a record?

segments.title: Curiosity, listening and respect in practice

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A question with a purpose. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, turned toward the two questions, one hand open toward the second.
on_screen: “Why are people from your community reluctant?”
“What part is difficult to use?”
scenes.narration: Curiosity is at the center of cultural humility, but not every question is curious in a useful way. Compare two questions from the readings. One asks, “Why are people from your community reluctant?” The other asks, “What part is difficult to use?” The first assigns a group explanation before the person speaks. The second points at the actual task and invites the person's own account. Professional curiosity is strongest when it has a clear purpose. A question about someone's whole cultural history may be interesting to you and still be unnecessary for the task. Before you ask, try a quick test. What will I do with the answer? If you cannot say, the question may be serving your interest more than the person's need.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Help without a story. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the white blouse, with curly hair (C3) stands full length, at ease, holding a printed sheet of travel times, as the person being served.
on_screen: A person can decline to share and still get practical help.
No one represents a whole community.
scenes.narration: Curiosity can also become a burden. In the readings, the staff member wants to understand the person he is serving better, so he asks about the family tradition behind seeking advice. She answers, “I would rather just compare the travel arrangements.” That is not a refusal of help or a sign of distrust. It tells him which question she wants answered now. So he goes back to the travel times and explains what the appointment process allows. If she later chooses to share more, he can listen, without assigning her account to everyone with a similar background. Practical help must never depend on someone sharing a personal story. And no one should be treated as the spokesperson for a culture. Hearing one person's account can improve your understanding of the moment. It does not tell you what a whole group wants.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A brief prepares your questions. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, holding a printed brief at his side.
on_screen: A brief prepares your questions.
It does not predict a person's answers.
scenes.narration: What about background reading? Community briefs can help. They introduce history, language and experiences with institutions that you might otherwise miss. The risk is using a brief as the answer. One reading names the trap directly: a claim about “how Hmong families are” turns background information into a stereotype. Reading that some communities value family involvement in planning does not tell you whom this person wants involved, what they wish to share, or whether the meeting arrangements work for them. So turn the background into open questions. Then listen for what fits, what differs and what is missing. Watch the premise in your wording too. In the bowl example, the researcher is tempted to ask the bowl's owner why she is not following the proper custom. That question already treats a pattern as a rule. Asking what matters to her about everyday use leaves her answer open.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Cultural opportunities. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, leaning forward slightly toward the viewer.
on_screen: Cultural opportunities: moments when identity comes to the front
No single identity explains a person.
scenes.narration: Hook and his colleagues add a useful idea. They call it cultural opportunities: moments in a conversation when someone's identity or background comes to the front. Noticing those moments, and choosing to explore them with care, is a skill people can learn. The same authors note that anxiety reduces curiosity. So part of the work is building comfort with these conversations, through practice and reflection rather than lectures. They also stress that no single identity explains a person. Someone is never only their language, their age, their faith or their disability. When an opening appears, ask one relevant question, and make it easy to decline: the person chooses what to share.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Being heard is not the same as influence. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, one hand on each side, as if weighing two things.
on_screen: Being heard is not the same as having influence.
Say what is decided, what is open and what the input can change.
scenes.narration: Listening and sharing influence are not the same thing. Go back to the two friends. The first friend owns the vehicle for the move and proposes leaving early. The second friend says the timing makes an important goodbye hard. The first friend says, “I understand,” and changes nothing. Listening happened. Influence did not. The first friend may have a real limit: the vehicle must be returned that afternoon. Humility does not mean promising an impossible schedule. It means separating the real limit from a preferred departure time, then exploring what is actually possible. Work has the same pattern. A supervisor announces an assignment, then asks the employee for ideas. The employee cannot tell what is still open. A clearer approach says what is decided, what remains open, and how a concern could affect the next step. Honest limits protect trust better than an invitation that cannot change anything.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Carrying a question forward. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the navy polo (C4) stands full length, holding a short printed summary, as the staff member who wrote it.
on_screen: Before: “The person has not made a decision.”
After: “The person wants to compare travel times with someone she trusts before choosing.”
scenes.narration: Finally, notice how your role shapes the encounter. Staff often choose the questions, the order of an explanation, the words in a record and the route a request takes. That is influence, even in an ordinary exchange. In the readings, the staff member writes a short summary for the staff who handle appointments. His first draft says, “The person has not made a decision.” That is accurate as far as it goes, but it leaves out her actual question. The next reader may simply send reminders to choose. His revision says she wants to compare travel conditions with someone she trusts before choosing, and that the allowed arrangements still need checking. Cultural humility asks you to look at that kind of influence, not give up the responsibility attached to it. The way you carry someone's question forward can keep their meaning or quietly lose it.

check.prompt: The person at the counter declines to talk about the family tradition behind her request and says she would rather just compare the travel arrangements. What should the staff member do?

options.text: Go back to the travel comparison, ask only questions that help with it, and leave room for her to share more later if she chooses.

feedback.text: You let her answer steer the conversation without treating it as a closed door. That keeps help available and leaves room for her to share more later if she chooses.
A line that works here: “Sure. Which travel times would be most helpful to look at together?”

options.text: Hold off on the options for now and gently ask once more about the tradition, since knowing her background would help him tailor them.

feedback.text: Pausing turns personal sharing into a condition for help. Returning to her actual question keeps both the help and her choice intact.
To her, it could feel like she has to explain her family before getting a straight answer about appointment times.

options.text: Add a note to her file that she seems wary of staff, so whoever helps her next is prepared and does not push the same questions.

feedback.text: A declined question can sting, and it is natural to look for a reason. Her reply did not supply distrust. Writing it down would carry an added meaning into the next conversation.
What did she actually say, word for word, and what would an accurate note contain?

reflection: Think of a question you often ask people you serve or work with. What do you do with the answer?
When did someone in a meeting ask for input on something already decided? How did it feel to be on the receiving end?
Where do you control the words in a record or summary that someone else will act on?

segments.title: When it goes wrong and how to recover

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Missed moments will happen. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, relaxed, with a small rueful smile.
on_screen: Missed opportunities will happen.
Repair without defensiveness is a core skill.
scenes.narration: The research says something plainly. You will miss things. Hook and his colleagues write that missed cultural opportunities and microaggressions will happen. What matters is what comes next. They name repairing those moments without defensiveness as a core skill. They also found that people judge their own humility poorly. You cannot see your blind spots by looking harder at yourself. That is why feedback from the people you serve, your peers and your supervisor matters so much. So the skill to build is recovering well.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A correction is information. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the coral blouse, with locs (C2) stands full length, speaking openly, one hand raised, as the second friend explaining the refusal.
on_screen: A correction is information.
“I heard the refusal as distance, and I understand that was not what you meant.”
scenes.narration: A correction gives you information your first interpretation missed. You might hear it at work as, “That is not why I asked,” or, “The explanation missed what matters to me.” In the friendship story, the second friend says, “I appreciated the offer. I wanted to manage the packing because accepting help would make me worry about owing you time you may need.” The first friend's rejection story now has clear contrary information. Look at how the first friend can respond: “I heard the refusal as distance, and I understand that was not what you meant.” That names the specific inference. It does not apologize for a whole identity. It does not ask the second friend for comfort. A further offer can stay open, with the second friend free to say no. A correction is about this person and this moment.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Three sideways repairs. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, turned toward the points, counting them off on one hand.
on_screen: Defending your intention
Asking for reassurance
Declaring it fixed
scenes.narration: Repairs tend to go sideways in three familiar ways. The first is defending your intention. You explain at length that you meant well. That may be true, but it does not address what you got wrong, and it can ask the other person to manage your feelings. The second is asking for reassurance. You need to hear that you are still a good person. That gives the other person more work at the very moment they told you something hard. The third is declaring it fixed. You apologized, so it must be resolved. But an apology is an action you took. Its effect on the other person is something you learn from them, over time. A sound repair is smaller and more specific. Name what you misunderstood. Ask whether your new understanding is accurate. Change what you can. Then leave the outcome open.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Where the first reading went. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, one hand raised, tracing a path in the air.
on_screen: Where did the first interpretation go?
A private change of mind may not reach a record or routine.
scenes.narration: Sometimes the hardest part of a repair is that the first interpretation has already traveled. One reading describes a service note that calls a person unwilling to involve others, when the person had only asked for one private conversation. That broad description could quietly reduce the support offered later. The same thing can happen at work. A newcomer who sent written comments instead of speaking in a meeting gets described as not committed, and that judgment shapes the assignments they are offered. So after a correction, ask where your account went. Is it in a note, a summary, a planning discussion or someone's memory of a meeting? If it is, a private change of mind will not undo its effects. Address it through the responsibility you have, keep the correction specific, and respect privacy.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A misunderstanding or a formal concern. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, upright and steady, speaking directly to the viewer.
on_screen: A misunderstanding and a formal allegation are not the same.
Supervisors and managers report protected-class allegations to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer immediately.
scenes.narration: One boundary needs to be clear. An ordinary misunderstanding and a formal concern are not the same thing. If someone alleges harassment or discrimination based on a protected characteristic, a reflective conversation or a private apology is not enough on its own, and it must never delay the required process. Under Minnesota Management and Budget Policy 1436, managers and supervisors report those allegations or incidents immediately to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow agency procedures. They do not wait for proof, for a group discussion or for their own reflection to finish. The readings give a wider rule as well. When a right, a complaint, a labor process, a safety duty or Tribal consultation is involved, contact the person or area responsible and follow its required process. Humility can shape how respectfully you respond. It never delays or replaces the duty itself.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Build comfort step by step. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the woman in the mauve hijab (C8) stands full length, relaxed, with an encouraging expression.
on_screen: Avoiding the subject leaves the old default in place.
Comfort grows with practice.
scenes.narration: After a misstep, a common reaction is to pull back. If asking caused trouble, maybe it is safer not to ask at all. In the friendship story, the first friend considers quietly withdrawing and never raising the offer again. That avoids an awkward moment, but it leaves the rejection story unexamined. Avoidance keeps the existing default untouched. Remember the finding that anxiety reduces curiosity. The answer is not to force yourself into hard conversations all at once. It is to build comfort step by step. Ask one relevant question with permission to decline. Notice one opening and respond to it. Each small, honest attempt makes the next one easier.

check.prompt: A colleague tells you, “That is not why I asked for the meeting to be moved.” You had told the team it was about avoiding a tough topic. What is the strongest next move?

options.text: Name the specific assumption you made, ask whether you now understand it correctly, and correct what you told the team.

feedback.text: You named the inference, checked your new understanding and followed it to where it traveled. That last step is the one people most often skip. Keep doing it.
Words that fit: “I assumed it was about the topic, and I was wrong. I will let the team know that was my guess, not your reason.”

options.text: Explain that you were only trying to help the team understand the change, so your colleague knows you meant well and were not criticizing them.

feedback.text: Your intention may well have been good. Opening with it, though, keeps the focus on you. Naming the assumption first addresses what your colleague actually raised.
Your colleague may now be wondering what the rest of the team believes about them. That question matters more to them than your intent.

options.text: Apologize warmly and sincerely, thank your colleague for telling you, and let the matter rest so it does not become a bigger deal for them.

feedback.text: Wanting a clean ending after an awkward moment is very human. An apology is a good start. The team still holds the wrong reason unless you correct it.
Where did your first explanation go, and who still believes it?

reflection: When someone last corrected your reading of them, what did you do in the first ten seconds?
Which of the three sideways repairs, defending, seeking reassurance or declaring it fixed, do you fall into most?
Who could give you honest feedback about how you come across across differences, and what would make it easy for them?

segments.title: Bringing it into your work

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A fact sheet is not a person. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, holding a printed analysis form at his side.
on_screen: A fact sheet is not a person.
A blank analysis is not humility.
scenes.narration: One reading describes a worker who refuses the Equity Analysis Toolkit because, as he puts it, humility is not a form. The readings disagree. Both are true at once. Learning about a community does not tell you what an individual wants, so you still need the conversation. And a structured process does a different job: it explains how a decision was made, whose experience informed it, and what benefits and burdens were weighed. A team can complete every field and still miss an important perspective. A team can also be very curious and never follow through. So use the analysis process that applies to the decision, and while you do, ask the people affected what the available information misses. One line from the readings sums it up: a fact sheet is not a person, and a blank analysis is not humility.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Arrangement or access. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, holding a clipboard with a checklist.
on_screen: A contract is an arrangement.
Access is what people can actually use.
scenes.narration: Checklists can support humility when the evidence behind each answer is examined. Here is a practice case from the readings. A team reviewing a service marks interpreter services as available, because a contract is in place. But no one has checked how people learn about the service, how requests get arranged, or what happens when an interpreter is not available. A contract establishes an arrangement. It does not show that a person could get interpretation that was timely and useful. The strong response is not to throw out the checklist. The strong response keeps the contract information, names the access questions that are still unanswered, and asks the people responsible for the service how those conditions are checked. The same goes for organizational self-assessments from the National Center for Cultural Competence. They help you examine conditions. They do not rate any one employee.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Partnership with honest limits. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the olive shirt, hair tied back (C7) stands full length, pointing to one line on a printed draft instruction, as the community member.
on_screen: Explain what input can change.
Do not hand staff work to the person who spoke up.
No one speaks for everyone.
scenes.narration: In one reading, a community member tells a staff member that a proposed instruction describes the route accurately but never says how to recognize the public entrance. The community member also describes the feeling of a service hidden behind insider knowledge. The staff member can learn from both. Partnership means asking which part should be clearer, explaining what staff can change, and offering the community member a chance to review the revision if they want one. It does not mean asking them to rewrite every letter or to speak for all service users. It also does not mean asking for a thank-you on an unchanged draft. That turns participation into endorsement. If staff hold the decision, say so honestly. Repeated invitations that collect stories without considering them use up people's time while the barrier stays in place.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Openness needs capacity. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, holding a sheet of discussion questions.
on_screen: A welcome is a statement.
A usable route takes time, information and a way to respond.
scenes.narration: Openness also needs capacity to matter. In a practice orientation from the readings, the coordinator tells newcomers they can ask questions freely. One participant explains that raising an unfinished question in front of the group can feel like challenging the facilitator before understanding their purpose. The participant would welcome time to think first. The coordinator had seen quick public questions as a sign of engagement. The participant's account changes that reading, and the coordinator does not need to decide what it says about the participant's identity. The coordinator can share the discussion questions ahead of time and explain the purpose of the activity. That only works if people get the questions in time and know how to respond. A promise nobody can keep is not capacity. The same pattern runs through the employee life cycle, from hiring to onboarding to supervision.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: A request needs no special words. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the sage shirt and glasses (C1) stands full length, holding a short written note, as the employee asking for written information.
on_screen: A request does not need special words.
Forward it promptly, and tell the person who asked who will decide.
scenes.narration: Keep real responsibilities clear, too. In one practice example, an employee tells a supervisor that hearing loss makes spoken briefings difficult and asks for written information. The employee never uses the words reasonable accommodation, and does not need to. Under the state's policy, whoever receives the request forwards it promptly to the person who decides. At the same time, they tell the employee who that is. Supervisors and managers do not ask for medical information or documentation. Requests for documentation belong to the agency ADA Coordinator. A learning conversation should never ask the employee to explain a diagnosis or put the adjustment to a team vote. Respect the employee's own description of what would help and let the actual process decide. The same applies to equity analysis for a real decision and to any formal process. Your reflection supports that work. It never replaces or delays it.

scenes.visual: White slide in the style of “The Water We Swim In”. Small caps label at the top left: PEOPLE, ACCESS AND CULTURE. Dark blue title: Learned, did, still unknown. The points appear on the left, one at a time. On the right, the man in the maroon polo (C6) stands full length, turned toward the three points, one hand open.
on_screen: Confirm the concern. Name who can act. Say how people will hear back.
Insight, action and effect are different claims.
scenes.narration: Last, follow through and describe it honestly. For any concern people raise, use a simple sequence. Confirm what you heard. Identify the role that can respond. Explain what will be considered and how people will learn what happened. Then set a date to come back to it. Without that, a team can record that engagement occurred while the barrier stays untouched. When you report what changed, keep three claims apart. What you learned, such as a new understanding of someone's meaning. What you did, such as a revised letter. And what the effect was, which needs its own evidence from the people affected. No new feedback does not prove the barrier disappeared. One thank-you does not prove it works for everyone. The Hook reading asks a good question here: how could your team build feedback loops so staff learn how people actually experience them? Keep the unanswered questions visible.

check.prompt: A service review marks interpreter services as available because a contract exists. No one has checked how people learn about it or what happens when no interpreter is free. What should the team do?

options.text: Keep the contract fact, list the open access questions, and ask the people responsible for the service how those conditions are checked.

feedback.text: You kept what is known and made the gap visible. Next, add a date to come back to the answer so the question does not quietly close.
Try framing it as: “The contract is in place. What do people experience when they ask for an interpreter, and how would anyone know?”

options.text: Treat the contract as enough evidence for this review, since it commits the provider to the service, and note access as a topic for next year.

feedback.text: The contract shows an arrangement exists. The stronger response asks whether people can actually use it, which is the question the checklist was pointing at.
For someone waiting at a counter without the words they need, a contract on file does not help unless the request works in that moment.

options.text: Stop using the checklist for this item, since a checked box cannot prove access, and replace it with an open discussion at the next team meeting.

feedback.text: Frustration with box-checking is common and often fair. The checklist still surfaced a useful question. The fix is evidence and follow-up, not dropping the tool.
Which checklist in your own work has a box that deserves a closer look?

reflection: Which structured tool in your work could do more if you asked the people affected what it misses?
Where have you seen people asked for input with no word afterward about what happened to it?
Pick one recent change you made. What did you learn, what did you do, and what do you still not know about its effect?

simulations.intro: Whatever your role at DHS, you have probably written or answered something that made perfect sense from the inside. In this scenario, you sit at a small team table where a letter is accurate and still not working for someone. You are a peer on the team, not its lead, so your influence comes from what you notice and what you say. Watch for the moment a correct answer starts standing in for a usable one.
simulations.title: The visitor letter
simulations.learner_role: You are a member of a small DHS team that keeps the appointment letter and web page up to date for people coming in person to a DHS building. You are a peer on the team, not its lead. Your teammates are an experienced teammate who has written the letter for years, a newer teammate who joined two months ago, and the team lead.
simulations.background: On Monday the team inbox gets an email from a visitor, a member of the public. She writes: “Your letter gave me the address, and I found the building. Then I walked around it twice. There were four doors and none of them said which one was for visitors. I almost went home and missed my appointment.” The team lead puts it on the agenda for Tuesday's team meeting. The letter has not changed in three years, and the experienced teammate checked the address against the official listing last spring. You have about twenty minutes of meeting time, a shared draft of the letter, and a team tracker where items are opened and closed.

decisions.setup: The team lead reads the visitor's email aloud. The experienced teammate speaks first: “The address is correct. I checked it myself. The directions are complete. People just need to read the letter.” The newer teammate is taking notes and says nothing. The team lead looks around the table and asks, “Thoughts?” Everyone turns toward you.
decisions.prompt: What do you say about the visitor's email?

choices.text: “The address was checked, so the letter is accurate. Let's send her a warm thank-you, confirm the address, and invite her to call if she gets lost again.”
choices.consequence: The experienced teammate agrees right away and offers to send the reply. The team lead hesitates, then says that sounds fine. The newer teammate starts to say something, then looks back down at the notes. The item is marked done in the tracker in under two minutes. Later that afternoon, the experienced teammate shares a draft reply in the team chat: “Thank you for your feedback. We have confirmed the address in our letter is correct. If you need help finding us, please call.” It has not been sent yet.

feedback.text: Confirming the address answers where the building is. The visitor was telling the team which door to use is unclear. A stronger move keeps the checked address and asks her where the route broke down.

Wanting to close an item that looks already solved is a very normal meeting instinct, especially when a trusted colleague has checked the facts. The catch is that accurate and usable are different questions.
If you were the one circling the building, what would that thank-you reply tell you?

choices.text: “The address is right, but her point is which door is the public one. Could someone ask her where it got confusing, and could two of us walk the route?”
choices.consequence: The experienced teammate pauses, then nods slowly. “Fair. The address and the door are two different things.” The team lead offers to reply to the visitor and ask which part of the route was unclear. The newer teammate looks up and adds quietly that the letter says to use the north entrance, but nothing outside says north. The experienced teammate had never noticed. The team lead writes two items on the whiteboard: ask the visitor, walk the route. The meeting moves on with the question still open instead of closed.

feedback.text: You kept your teammate's checked fact and the visitor's experience side by side, and you turned the concern into two concrete next steps. Notice that your question gave the newer teammate an opening too. Keep looking for who else in the room has knowledge the discussion has not reached yet.
For the visitor, a reply asking where it got confusing says her walk around the building counted for something. That is very different from being told the address is correct.
When you walk the route, go in as someone who has never been there. Try to find the visitor door using only the letter, then note the exact point where you have to guess.

choices.text: “If she got lost, others probably did too. Let's rewrite the letter from scratch and redo the web page this week, so we fix every gap at once.”
choices.consequence: The team lead likes the energy but looks uncertain. The experienced teammate crosses his arms. “One email and the whole letter is broken?” The discussion turns into a debate about workload and who has time to rewrite everything. Nobody asks the visitor anything. The newer teammate stays quiet. The team lead ends by asking everyone to send comments on the current letter by Friday, when she will decide how much to change. The door question is still there, now buried under a bigger argument.

feedback.text: Taking a concern seriously enough to want a full fix is a caring reaction. One account shows a real gap; it does not yet show what every visitor needs or that everything else is wrong.

A stronger move starts with the specific difficulty the visitor named, which door, and finds out more before sizing the change. That also keeps the experienced teammate's knowledge of the letter in the conversation.
To the experienced teammate, “rewrite it from scratch” can sound like years of careful work dismissed. He may defend the letter instead of looking at the door problem.

choices.text: “Before we change anything, do we know anything about her? Maybe she's new to the area, or English isn't her first language. That would tell us who we should write for.”
choices.consequence: There is a short silence. The experienced teammate says, “Could be. Most people find it fine.” The team lead says the email does not say anything about that. The newer teammate frowns slightly but does not speak. The conversation drifts toward guessing about the visitor instead of looking at the doors. The item ends with the experienced teammate offering to send a polite reply confirming the address. The visitor's actual point, that four doors look the same, never gets discussed.

feedback.text: Guessing at the visitor's background puts the explanation inside her before she has said anything about herself. Asking which part of the route was unclear points at the letter, which the team can actually change.
The visitor wrote clearly about four unmarked doors. If she learned the team spent its time guessing about her instead, she might not bother writing next time.
What did the visitor's email actually say, and what did your question add to it?

decisions.setup: Wednesday morning, the newer teammate sends the team written comments on the draft letter. They are careful and specific, and they go further than anything said in the meeting: no sign outside says north even though the letter tells visitors to use the north entrance; visitors arriving by bus come from the opposite side; and the web page photo shows a door that was replaced last year. Twenty minutes later the experienced teammate replies to everyone: “Good points, but this is the kind of thing to raise in the meeting. People who care about this speak up in the room.” The team lead has not responded. The letter decision is not due until Friday.
decisions.prompt: How do you respond to the thread?

choices.text: Stay out of the thread so it does not turn into an argument, and message the newer teammate privately: “Don't worry about him, that's just how he is. Your comments were great.”
choices.consequence: The newer teammate thanks you and seems relieved. On the thread, though, nobody answers the experienced teammate, and his message stands as the team's last word. The team lead finally replies that she will look at the comments. By Thursday, only the photo fix has made it into the draft. The bus-side point is still sitting in an email, and the newer teammate does not send written comments on the next item.

feedback.text: Supporting a colleague privately is kind, and avoiding a public disagreement feels safer. It helped your teammate feel better, but the expectation stated in the thread is still unanswered where the whole team saw it.
A stronger response does both: it speaks to the content and the real deadline in the thread, then checks in privately. That way the useful input actually changes the letter.
A short public line can do a lot: “Written comments work for me. The decision isn't until Friday. The bus-side point is worth adding.”

choices.text: Reply in the thread: the north-sign and bus-side points are useful, and written comments work for a Friday decision, so fold them in. Then check in with the newer teammate privately.
choices.consequence: The team lead replies within the hour: “Agreed. Friday is the deadline, and written comments work.” The experienced teammate answers more slowly, then adds a thumbs-up and a question about the bus stop. When you check in privately, the newer teammate says the meeting moved too fast to check the building map, and writing it up was the best way to get it right. They ask whether the agenda could go out earlier next time. The bus-side detail goes into the draft.

feedback.text: You separated the real work need, useful input before Friday, from a familiar style of contributing, and you asked your teammate directly instead of guessing why. Build on it by suggesting the agenda change they raised, so the next newcomer does not have to ask.
For a newer teammate two months in, a public note about the content signals that careful written work counts here. A private check-in shows someone noticed without making them the topic.
Compared with simply reassuring your teammate in private, this response also addresses the expectation in front of the team, where it was stated.

choices.text: Reply to keep things moving: “Good points, and it does help to hear these in the meeting. Next time, just jump in so we can discuss them live.”
choices.consequence: The experienced teammate reacts with a thumbs-up. The team lead says nothing. The newer teammate replies with a short “Okay, will do” and does not add anything else to the thread. The north-sign and bus-side points sit in the thread without anyone acting on them. That afternoon, you pass the newer teammate in the hallway, and they stop you.

feedback.text: The team needed useful input before Friday, and your teammate delivered it. Backing a speak-in-the-room rule treats one style as the measure of commitment. A stronger reply addresses what they found and whether written comments meet the need.
To the newer teammate, this thread may read as: careful work gets criticized for its format. That lesson can follow a newcomer into supervision and the assignments they are offered.
Where did you learn that speaking up in the room shows you care? Does it fit every useful way of contributing?

choices.text: Message the experienced teammate privately to calm things down: “Go easy on our new teammate. They probably come from a background where people don't speak up in meetings, so writing felt safer.”
choices.consequence: The experienced teammate writes back, “Oh, I didn't realize. I'll keep that in mind,” and softens his tone in the next message. The thread moves on. But now he has an explanation for the newer teammate's comments that the newer teammate never gave. A few days later, he mentions to the team lead that the newer teammate may not be comfortable presenting, so maybe someone else should take the next presentation. The newer teammate hears about it secondhand and comes to find you near the elevators.

feedback.text: You wanted to protect your teammate, and the tone did soften. But the explanation came from a guess about a group, not from the person. Asking them directly, and addressing whether written comments meet the need, would not leave a new label behind.
From the newer teammate's side, a colleague has explained their behavior to others using an identity, without asking. It has already shaped who gets the next presentation.
What did the newer teammate actually do, and what reason did you add to it?

decisions.setup: That afternoon, the experienced teammate's draft reply to the visitor appears in the team chat: “Thank you for your feedback. We have confirmed the address in our letter is correct. If you need help finding us, please call.” The team lead reacts with a thumbs-up. Before it goes out, you reread the visitor's email. She never said the address was wrong. She said four doors looked the same. You still have a moment before the reply is sent.
decisions.prompt: Do you say anything about the draft reply?

choices.text: Post in the chat: “I reread her email. She found the building; it was the door she couldn't find. Could the reply ask which door she tried?”
choices.consequence: The experienced teammate replies after a few minutes: “Huh, you're right. I read it fast.” He rewrites the reply to thank the visitor and ask which door she tried first and what sign or detail would have helped. The team lead reopens the item in the tracker, shares the letter as a draft, and asks for comments by Friday. The newer teammate reacts to your message with a check mark and sends you a private note: “Glad you said that. The north entrance thing always confused me too.”

feedback.text: You went back to the visitor's actual words and offered your teammate a way to adjust without losing face. That is a recovery in real time. Next time, try raising the distinction in the meeting itself, while the whole team is there to hear it.
For the experienced teammate, a specific, friendly pointer to what the email said is much easier to act on than being told he got it wrong.

choices.text: Let it go. The experienced teammate has handled this letter for years, the meeting already decided, and reopening it now could leave him feeling second-guessed in front of the team lead.
choices.consequence: The experienced teammate sends the reply. The next morning, the visitor writes back: “I know the address is right. I said I couldn't find the door.” The team lead reopens the item, shares the letter as a draft, and asks for comments by Friday. The visitor is now a little less sure anyone is listening.

feedback.text: Deferring to an experienced colleague and a meeting decision is a very common choice, and it often feels like the respectful one. Here it let an answer to the wrong question reach the person who raised the concern.
A low-key way in next time: “Quick check before this goes. I think her point was about the door, not the address. Worth a question back to her?”

decisions.setup: The newer teammate stops you in the hallway. “Can I tell you something? I wrote my comments instead of talking because I needed to check the building map and the bus routes first. I didn't want to say something wrong about the entrances in front of everyone. And now it feels like people have decided something about me.” They wait for your response.
decisions.prompt: What do you say to the newer teammate?

choices.text: “I am so sorry. I really was just trying to help the thread move along. I hope you know I am on your side, and I would never want you to feel singled out.”
choices.consequence: The newer teammate says, “I know,” and the conversation ends politely. You feel better. But nothing in the thread changes, and the speak-in-the-room expectation stands as the team's last word. The bus-side point still has not made it into the draft. The newer teammate is friendly with you afterward but keeps comments short and verbal from then on.

feedback.text: Your apology was sincere, but it centered your intention and asked your teammate for reassurance. Naming the specific mistaken reading, and fixing it where it traveled, would address what they actually raised.
Try: “I got that wrong. You were checking facts, not holding back. Can I correct what I said in the thread? What would you want said?” Short, specific and about the action.
Reaching for your good intentions when you learn you caused harm is one of the most common reactions there is. Notice the pull, then turn back to what you were just told.

choices.text: “Thank you for telling me. I got that wrong: it was about checking your facts, not speaking up. I'd like to correct what I said. What would you want said?”
choices.consequence: The newer teammate nods. “Yes. Just that written comments are a real way to contribute.” You post a short note in the thread: you were wrong to say “just jump in,” the north-sign and bus-side points are solid, and written comments are a real way to contribute to a Friday decision. The team lead adds that she will send agendas a day ahead from now on. The experienced teammate replies with a question about the bus stop. The draft picks up the bus-side detail.

feedback.text: You named the specific thing you got wrong, did not ask for reassurance, and asked what your teammate wanted said before saying anything. Then you corrected it where the impression formed. How it lands for them is something you will learn over time. Keep the habit of asking what else needs correcting.

For the newer teammate, a correction that reaches the thread matters more than a private apology, because the thread is where the impression formed. Being asked first also leaves them in charge of what the team hears about their reasons.

decisions.setup: The newer teammate stops you near the elevators. “Can I tell you something? I heard you told him I come from a background where people don't speak up. That isn't why I wrote my comments instead of talking. I needed to check the building map and the bus routes first. Now someone else is doing the next presentation, and it feels like people have decided something about me.” They wait for your response.
decisions.prompt: What do you say to the newer teammate?

choices.text: “I am so sorry. I was only trying to get him to ease up on you. I hope you know I am on your side, and I never meant it as criticism.”
choices.consequence: The newer teammate says, “I know,” and the conversation ends politely. You feel better. But the experienced teammate still believes the reason you gave him, and the next presentation stays with someone else. The bus-side point still has not made it into the draft. The newer teammate is friendly with you afterward but keeps comments short and verbal from then on.

feedback.text: Your apology was sincere, but it centered your intention and asked your teammate for reassurance. Naming the guess you passed on, and correcting it with the person who heard it, would address what they actually raised.
Try: “I got that wrong. I guessed a reason and passed it on. I'd like to tell him it was my guess. Is that okay with you?” Short, specific and about the action.
Reaching for your good intentions when you learn you caused harm is one of the most common reactions there is. Notice the pull, then turn back to what you were just told.

choices.text: “Thank you for telling me. I got it wrong: I guessed a reason and passed it on. Can I tell him it was my guess? What else should I correct?”
choices.consequence: The newer teammate nods. “Tell him. And I'd like a fair shot at presenting.” You tell the experienced teammate directly that the reason you gave him was your guess, not something your teammate said, and that it was wrong. You leave your teammate's own reasons for them to share. He says he will tell the team lead that the newer teammate wants to present. He also replies in the thread with a question about the bus stop, and the draft picks up the bus-side detail.

feedback.text: You named the specific guess you made, did not ask for reassurance, and took the correction to the experienced teammate, where the label had traveled. You let your teammate decide what else was said. How it lands for them is something you will learn over time. Keep asking what else needs correcting.
For the newer teammate, knowing the experienced teammate was told the reason was a guess matters more than a private apology, because that guess was already shaping who presents.

decisions.setup: By Friday the revised letter is ready. It names the visitor door by what you see, the one with the blue awning facing the parking lot, and has an updated photo. The team also learned that no sign outside the building says Visitors; signs are handled by the building's facilities staff, not your team. The experienced teammate suggests marking the visitor's item closed in the tracker as feedback addressed, and sending her a thank-you. The team lead asks what you think before she decides.
decisions.prompt: What do you suggest for closing the loop?

choices.text: “The letter is fixed, so mark it closed, and send her a thank-you that lists exactly what changed in the letter, so she knows her email made a difference.”
choices.consequence: The item turns green in the tracker. The visitor gets a thank-you that lists the letter changes, and it reads well. But nobody owns the sign request, so it never gets sent, and nobody asks the visitor whether the new wording would have worked. Two months later, the front desk mentions that visitors still ask which door is the public one. No one on the team connects it to the closed item.

feedback.text: Revising the letter was a real action, and listing the changes for the visitor was a good touch. Whether visitors can now find the door is a separate question that needs its own evidence. Keeping that question open, and naming who owns the sign, would have caught the gap.
Closing an item feels like progress, and tidy trackers help teams function. The risk is treating a finished task as proof that the barrier is gone.
What would you need to hear from visitors to say the door problem is actually solved?

choices.text: “Tell her what changed and what went to facilities, ask if the new wording would have helped, and keep ‘does it work?’ open in the tracker.”
choices.consequence: The team lead likes it and asks the experienced teammate to send the sign request to facilities. The reply to the visitor thanks her, explains the new wording, says the sign question has gone to the people responsible for building signs, and asks whether the revision would have gotten her to the right door. A week later the visitor answers: the blue awning detail would have helped, though from the sidewalk the awning is hidden behind a tree until you are almost at the door. The team has a next step, and a member of the public who knows she was heard.

feedback.text: You kept three things apart: what the team changed, what belongs to someone else, and whether it actually works for visitors. Asking the visitor directly is what turned up the hidden awning. Set a date to check the sign request, too.
For the visitor, hearing what changed and what did not, and being asked again, shows her contribution did something. That makes it more likely she, and others, will speak up next time.
Consider adding one line to the tracker for the next review: ask the front desk whether visitors still ask which door to use.

choices.text: “Let's tell her a new Visitors sign is going up. She circled the building twice, and a firm promise shows her we took it seriously.”
choices.consequence: The visitor replies warmly and thanks the team. Then the experienced teammate contacts facilities, who explain that exterior signs go through a review and may take months, if they are approved at all. The team lead has to decide whether to write to the visitor again and walk the promise back. The revised letter is a real improvement, but the team now has a commitment it does not control.
