choices.consequence: You say, “I put my view out first. That may have made it harder to disagree. The direction is open until this team decides. What have your teams heard that I have not?” There is a pause. Then the county partnerships director speaks. County staff tell her that many people renew with help from a worker at a library or a county lobby. They do not have reliable internet at home, or they do not know the portal. The operations director adds that the listening session notes mention the same thing more than once. Nobody had wanted to be the one to slow down your item. Now the concern is in the room, with time left to ask what evidence is still needed.

feedback.text: You named your own influence out loud. A senior leader’s view, said first, shapes what people feel free to say. Calling your view a lean, and asking what teams have heard, turned an invitation to speak into a real chance to shape the choice. Build on it by saying what kind of concern could change the plan, and asking for evidence, not only opinions.

To a director, an assistant commissioner’s lean can sound like the answer. The county partnerships director had the access concern all along. Your question gave her a reason to believe it could matter, not just be heard.
In your own leadership meetings, how often do you share your view before you have heard the room? What do you lose when you do?

choices.text: Ask the table directly, “Does anyone disagree, or see a risk I have missed?” Wait a full moment so people have time. When no one speaks up, move on.
choices.consequence: You ask, and the room stays still. The operations director says, “No, it makes sense.” The question was sincere. But it asked people to stand against your stated view in front of their peers, with no sign that a concern could change anything. The item moves forward. The county partnerships director says nothing, and later sends you a private note about an access concern from county staff.

feedback.text: “Does anyone disagree?” asks people to oppose a stated view. “What have your teams heard that the numbers might miss?” asks for knowledge. The second gives people a reason to speak that does not feel like a challenge.
Next time, say what is decided, what is open, and what would change your mind. For example: “I lean toward this. Here is what would change my view. What have you heard?”

choices.text: Withdraw the item for now. Tell the team you will not bring any proposal forward until every affected community has reviewed it and endorsed it.
choices.consequence: The directors are surprised. The operations director asks what endorsement would look like and who would give it. No one knows. The item misses the internal deadline. Staff who spent months on the analysis feel the work was dropped, not examined. And the access concern the county partnerships director had in mind is never named, because the meeting ends on the withdrawal instead of on what people have heard.

feedback.text: Not wanting the agency to move ahead of the people affected is a sound instinct. The trouble is that endorsement is not the test of useful participation. Partnership asks how input will be used, not whether everyone signs off.
A stronger move keeps the proposal open and asks what evidence is missing. That lets a real concern change the plan, or not, for stated reasons.
To your directors, a sudden withdrawal can feel like their analysis did not count. They needed to know what you wanted examined.

decisions.setup: The item is going forward. After the listening sessions, staff added phone and in-person help to the plan. They are still working out how people who renew with help will be reached. Next week you testify at a legislative hearing. The communications lead sends a draft opening line: “This proposal was developed in partnership with the communities it serves, and no one will lose access.”
decisions.prompt: What do you want the public record to say about how this proposal was developed and what it will do?

choices.text: Rewrite the line to name who was heard, what changed because of it, what you do not know yet, and when you will report back.
choices.consequence: Your opening says: “Listening sessions with people who use the program, counties and advocates raised concerns about online-only renewal. After those sessions, staff added phone and in-person help to the plan. The agency does not yet know how well that will work for people without reliable internet. The administration will report on renewals through assisted channels after six months.” A legislator asks how many people that is. You say you do not know yet, and how you will find out. The answer is less smooth than the draft. People in the room who sat in the listening sessions hear their concern named in the record.

feedback.text: You kept three things apart: what was heard, what was done, and what effect is still unknown. That is more accurate than “partnership,” and it can be checked. Build on it by making sure the six-month report goes back to the people who raised the concern.
To someone who attended a listening session, “no one will lose access” is a claim they may know is unproven. Hearing their concern named, with an honest unknown, tells them it was taken seriously.
Which claims in your public statements describe effort, and which describe effect? Do you have evidence for the second kind?

choices.text: Keep the communications lead’s line. It is the message leadership has approved, legislators expect a clear position, and a hearing is not the place to raise doubts about your own proposal.
choices.consequence: The hearing goes smoothly. Two weeks later, an advocate who attended a listening session testifies at another hearing. He says he told the agency online-first renewal would shut people out, and now hears it described as partnership. A reporter quotes him. “No one will lose access” is now the agency’s position to defend, without evidence behind it.

feedback.text: Under public pressure, a confident line can feel like the safe choice. The risk is that a claim of partnership, or of no harm, says more than the evidence shows. Honest limits often protect trust better than reassurance.

Compare “developed in partnership” with “people raised this concern, here is what changed, here is what is still unknown.” The second claims less and holds up better when someone who was in the room speaks.

choices.text: Cut the partnership phrase, which overstates what the listening sessions were, but keep “no one will lose access,” since phone and in-person help will remain in the plan.
choices.consequence: The opening is shorter. A legislator asks how the agency knows no one will lose access. You point to phone and in-person help. She asks how many people will need it and whether it is funded for that many. You do not have those numbers. The help exists as an arrangement. Whether people can use it is still unknown, and the record now says otherwise.

feedback.text: Dropping the partnership claim was a step toward accuracy. “No one will lose access” still treats an arrangement as proof of an effect. Help that exists is not the same as help people can reach.
Separate the arrangement from the result: “Phone and in-person help will stay. The agency will check whether people who need it can use it, and report back by a set date.”

choices.text: Keep the partnership phrase, and replace “no one will lose access” with a note that phone and in-person help will remain, so the claim has something concrete behind it.
choices.consequence: Your opening says the proposal was developed in partnership, and that phone and in-person help will remain. The hearing goes smoothly. A week later, an advocate who spoke at a listening session writes to the committee. He says he was asked for his view once and never heard what it changed. Calling that partnership, he writes, claims more than happened. Adding a detail about help did not change what the word claimed.

feedback.text: Adding something concrete was a real step. But the detail supports a different claim. “Partnership” describes how the proposal was developed, and partnership asks how input will be used, not only whether it was collected. Saying who was heard and what changed claims only what happened.
To someone who spoke at a listening session, “partnership” is a claim about his part in it. He knows whether anyone told him what his input could change.
When you describe how a proposal was developed, would the people who took part use the same word?

decisions.setup: The county partnerships director’s note is in your inbox. County staff in several regions say many people renew with help from a worker at a library or county lobby, because they lack reliable internet or do not know the portal. She adds, “I did not want to be the one to slow this down.” The item has not yet gone to the commissioner.
decisions.prompt: The concern reached you after the meeting where it could have shaped the choice. What do you do with it now?

choices.text: Thank the county partnerships director for the concern. Put the item back on the next leadership agenda, say why, and ask staff to add what people who renew with help have said.
choices.consequence: At the next meeting you say, “I moved too fast. A concern reached me after the meeting that I should have heard in the room. The item is open again until the access question is examined.” Staff pull the listening session notes. The same concern appears in four sessions. It had been summed up as “some technology questions.” Now it is a named question with evidence behind it, and your directors have seen a late concern change your plan.

feedback.text: You treated a late concern as information, not as a problem with her timing. Saying in front of the team why the item reopened shows directors that speaking up can change things. Next, ask her what made it hard to say in the room.
For the county partnerships director, a public reopening without blame answers the question, “Is it safe to raise this?” Others on the team are watching for the same answer.

choices.text: Thank the county partnerships director and say the point helps. Have staff add it as an appendix after the item goes to the commissioner, so the timeline holds and it is on record.
choices.consequence: Staff add a short line: “Some participants raised technology access.” The proposal does not change. The county partnerships director reads the line and sees her concern turned into a footnote. She tells her deputy that next time she will not bother.

feedback.text: An appendix after the decision hears the concern but gives it no room to shape the choice. Putting it on the agenda while the item is open lets it inform the decision, even if the decision stays the same.
When a concern arrives late, what tells you whether it can still change something?

choices.text: Ask the county partnerships director to have county staff present the concern to the leadership team themselves, with a full alternative plan, so the team hears it from the source.
choices.consequence: County staff are asked to build a plan for a state program they do not run. Two decline. One prepares slides on her own time. The concern gets a hearing, but the people who raised it carried the agency’s work to get there, and they notice.

feedback.text: Wanting to hear a concern from its source is reasonable. Asking contributors to produce the solution shifts staff work onto them. Partnership values what they know without making them responsible for the fix.
Ask your own staff to examine the concern. Then invite county staff to review a revision if they wish, and tell them what their review can change.

decisions.setup: Three days after the hearing, a health director for a Tribal Nation writes to the commissioner. The letter says the renewal change will affect many of the Nation’s members, and the Nation was not consulted. The operations director points out that a Tribal member attended one listening session. She suggests replying that Tribal input was gathered. The response is yours to handle.
decisions.prompt: The letter names a gap in how the agency worked with a Tribal Nation. How do you respond?

choices.text: Name the gap without defending the process. Call the person responsible for Tribal consultation, let them say what the process requires, and draft the reply to the Nation with them.
choices.consequence: You do not reply that input was gathered. You call the person responsible for Tribal consultation at DHS that day. They explain that the listening sessions were not consultation with the Nation, and walk you through the required process and timing. You draft the reply with them. It says plainly that the agency held listening sessions but has not consulted with the Nation. It names who will follow up, which parts of the renewal plan can still change before rollout, and when the Nation will hear about a first meeting. The health director replies briefly to confirm. Nothing is resolved yet. The relationship has a real next step instead of a defense.

feedback.text: You named the gap plainly and sent it to the person and process built for it. That keeps Tribal consultation with the people responsible for it. Build on it by asking, at the start of your next change item, where Tribal consultation fits in the timeline.

To the health director, “Tribal input was gathered” would have turned one person at an open session into a stand-in for a Nation. An honest account, with a date, gives the Nation something real to respond to.

Before a reply like this, call the person responsible for Tribal consultation. Then try words like: “The agency held listening sessions. That was not consultation with the Nation. Here is who will follow up, what can still change, and when.”

choices.text: Use the operations director’s suggestion. Reply that a Tribal member took part in the listening sessions, that this input was considered, and that the agency welcomes further comment from the Nation.
choices.consequence: The reply goes out. The health director writes back within a day. One person attending an open session does not speak for the Nation, he says, and the agency knows the difference. The commissioner is copied. What began as a gap in consultation is now a question of whether DHS takes its responsibilities to Tribal Nations seriously.

feedback.text: Compare this with naming the gap and calling the person responsible for Tribal consultation. That reply claims less and opens the required process. This one asks one person to stand in for a whole Nation, which no participant should have to do.

Under time pressure, it is tempting to point to the input that does exist. But being invited to an open session is different from consultation with a Nation. Saying so plainly protects trust better than a stretched claim.

choices.text: Reply quickly and warmly. Thank the Nation for raising its concern, say its feedback matters, and promise it will be considered as the change rolls out, so the letter is not left waiting.
choices.consequence: The letter is polite. It does not say what can change, who will follow up, or when. The health director replies asking for a meeting, not more thanks. Weeks pass while staff wonder who owns the response. The rollout date gets closer, and the Nation still does not know what is open.

feedback.text: Thanks and a promise to consider are not a next step. A stronger reply says what is decided, what is open, who will follow up, and by when.
When a partner tells you they were left out, what do you owe them in your first reply?

choices.text: Ask the budget analyst, a Native staff member in your administration, what he thinks the Tribes want, and draft the reply from his view before it goes to the commissioner.
choices.consequence: The budget analyst is caught off guard. He works on budget forecasting, not Tribal relations. He says he can share his own view, but he cannot speak for any Nation, let alone all of them. He leaves feeling he was asked because of who he is, not what he does. The letter still has no answer, and the required process has not started.

feedback.text: To the budget analyst, this request turns his identity into an assignment. No one should be asked to represent an entire community, and a staff member is not a Tribal government.
The stronger path goes to the person responsible for Tribal consultation, who says what the process requires and drafts the reply with you. That respects both the budget analyst and the Nation.
Who in your administration gets asked to explain a community because of who they are? What would it take to stop?

practiced: Naming your own influence when you share a view before the room has spoken
Saying what is decided, what is open, and what kind of concern could change the plan
Treating silence after a senior leader speaks as missing information, not agreement
Making public claims that keep what was heard, what was done, and what is still unknown apart
Sending Tribal consultation to the person or area responsible and its required process
Never asking one person to speak for a whole community or Nation
this_week: Before your next leadership meeting, decide whether to share your view first or last. If first, say what would change your mind.
Read one public statement your administration is about to make. Mark each claim as effort or effect, and check the evidence behind each effect claim.
Ask one director how your administration measures engagement. Do the measures count meetings, or show whether input changed a decision?
Find out who handles Tribal consultation for your administration’s work, and where it enters your planning timeline.

simulations.intro: If you manage grants or contracts, the requirements you inherit decide who can even apply. I have watched small organizations that families trust give up before the deadline. In this version, you answer an applicant’s question, guide a review panel and debrief an applicant who was not funded.

cast.label: the person responsible for grants policy

simulations.title: Who Can Apply
simulations.learner_role: You are the grant manager for a new DHS grant program. You answer applicants’ questions during the solicitation, run the review panel and debrief applicants afterward. Grants policy, legal requirements and the final award decision belong to the person or area responsible; you shape how questions are answered and how the review is carried out.
simulations.background: The program will fund community organizations to help families find and keep the services they qualify for. The solicitation was built from an older one used for larger statewide contracts. It asks for three years of audited financial statements, a 25-page narrative and upload through the online grants portal only. The question period is open for two more weeks. Several of the organizations the program most hopes to reach have small staffs and have never held a state grant.

decisions.setup: The director of a community organization with four staff writes in during the question period. His organization has reviewed financial statements, not audited ones. Writing 25 pages will take his staff away from families for weeks, and the portal will not accept the file format his bookkeeper uses. He asks: “Can an organization like ours apply?”
decisions.prompt: How do you answer?

choices.text: Answer that the requirements apply to every applicant equally, so changing them for one would be unfair, and point him to the pages of the solicitation that explain each one.
choices.consequence: Your answer is accurate to the document. Two days pass with no reply. If nothing changes, almost every proposal will come from organizations that have held state grants before.

feedback.text: Treating every applicant the same feels fair, and consistency matters in public money. The readings point out that equal wording does not give equal access to the knowledge or resources needed to use it. Valuing consistency and checking a requirement’s purpose can go together.
Compare pointing to the pages with asking which of these requirements are real and which were carried over from an older solicitation. The first defends the document; the second examines it.
From the director’s side, the answer confirms what he suspected: the grant was not written with organizations like his in mind.

choices.text: Find out which requirements come from grants policy or law and which were copied from the older solicitation. Ask the person or area responsible, and post the answer for everyone.
choices.consequence: The person responsible for grants policy confirms that, for this program, the financial review can use statements like the director’s; the audit requirement had been copied from the larger contracts. The page count and portal-only upload were carried over, not required. The program issues an addendum: a shorter narrative, a second way to submit, and a plain explanation of the financial review. Every applicant sees it, not only the director. He writes back that his organization will apply.

feedback.text: You separated the real requirement from the habits that grew around it, then used the route that can actually change them. Publishing the answer to everyone kept the process fair while making it usable. Keep asking that question of every requirement you inherit.
When you send the addendum, say what changed and what did not, and why. People trust a limit they can understand.

choices.text: Tell the director the audit requirement looks like a holdover from the larger contracts, so you can waive it for small organizations like his, and he should start writing his proposal now.
choices.consequence: The director thanks you and starts writing. An hour later, the person responsible for grants policy tells you a waiver for one applicant would be unfair to others and would have to go through an addendum. You write to the director that your answer was not yours to give.

feedback.text: Your instinct, to remove a barrier, was right. The promise came before checking authority. The stronger choice takes the same question through the person or area responsible so the answer holds and reaches every applicant.
Try: “That is a fair question. I will find out which of these are required for this grant and post the answer for all applicants by Friday.”

choices.text: Suggest the director partner with a larger organization as the lead applicant, since small community groups often struggle to manage state grants and the reporting that comes with them.
choices.consequence: The director replies that his organization has managed private grants for ten years and that families come to them because they are not a large agency. He asks whether the program wants organizations like his or not.

feedback.text: The director asked about the requirements, and the answer was about his organization’s ability. From his side, a general belief about small groups replaced a question about his actual situation.
The stronger choice examines the solicitation before deciding what an applicant can or cannot manage. Ask what he has, not what groups like his usually lack.
What did you assume about the director’s organization before he told you anything about it?

decisions.setup: You facilitate the review panel. Proposal 14 is from the director’s organization. The first reviewer says it “doesn’t read as professional,” and that its plan to reach families through gatherings at a community center and home visits by trusted neighbors is “unproven.” The second reviewer answers, “I know that community. They won’t go to a formal clinic anyway, so this makes sense.” The published criteria cover need, approach, capacity and budget. Nothing in them mentions writing style.
decisions.prompt: How do you guide the panel?

choices.text: Bring the panel back to the published criteria. Ask both reviewers, critical and approving alike, what in the proposal supports their view.
choices.consequence: You note that writing style is not a criterion, and that neither “professional” nor a belief about a community is evidence. The first reviewer points to the approach section and admits the plan is described clearly, just not in the language he is used to. The second reviewer finds the proposal’s own data on how families found them last year, which is stronger than her general view. The panel scores the approach on what the applicant wrote. The first reviewer still has questions about capacity, and those go into the notes as questions for the applicant.

feedback.text: You caught both shortcuts, the unfavorable one and the favorable one. A belief about a community, even a sympathetic one, is still a profile standing in for the applicant’s own account. Keep using the proposal as the evidence.
Consider the applicant who wrote Proposal 14. They described their approach in their own words. Your question let the panel read those words instead of a reviewer’s idea of the community.

choices.text: Let each reviewer score independently, as the panel process expects. Steering the discussion could bias the scores, and the comments will speak for themselves.
choices.consequence: The scores come in far apart. The first reviewer scores the approach low with the comment “unprofessional tone.” The second reviewer scores it high with “culturally appropriate for this community.” Neither comment refers to what the proposal says.

feedback.text: Independence in scoring matters, and you can keep it. Facilitating can still mean asking every reviewer to tie a comment to a criterion and to the proposal. That is part of running a fair review.
What does a comment like “unprofessional tone” measure, and which criterion does it belong to?

choices.text: Agree with the second reviewer. She knows the community well, and her view balances the first reviewer’s concern about the plan, so the score reflects both sides.
choices.consequence: The first reviewer goes quiet and scores as he planned. The second reviewer’s statement about the community goes into the notes as the reason for the high score. If the applicant ever reads those notes, they will find a description of their community that they never gave.

feedback.text: It is common to treat a favorable generalization as the fix for an unfavorable one. The readings treat both the same way: a claim about how a community is turns background into a stereotype. The proposal is the account that counts.
Ask the second reviewer, “What in the proposal shows that?” and the first reviewer, “Which criterion does your concern fall under?” Then both views stand on the same evidence.

choices.text: Let the discussion go to keep the panel on schedule, then quietly raise Proposal 14’s approach score afterward to balance the first reviewer’s low one.
choices.consequence: As you open the score sheet, the second reviewer asks what you are changing. It is not your role to change a reviewer’s score. If you did, the whole panel’s results for this proposal would have to be checked again. The first reviewer’s comment is still in the file.

feedback.text: You noticed a real problem in the review. The fix stepped outside your authority and made the review harder to defend. The stronger choice addresses the comment in the room, through the panel process.
From the other applicants’ side, a score changed by the grant manager is exactly the kind of unfairness the process exists to prevent.

decisions.setup: Awards are announced. The director’s organization scored well on approach but was not funded; capacity scores were lower. In the debrief call he says, “This process rewards organizations that can pay grant writers. Families trust us. That didn’t count.” You can explain the scores. The next solicitation is being drafted now by another team.
decisions.prompt: How do you respond, and what happens to his point?

choices.text: Acknowledge his point without defending the process. Explain each criterion’s score, take his point to the team drafting the next solicitation, and say when he will hear.
choices.consequence: The director is still disappointed, and says so. He also says it helps to hear that the approach scored well and where capacity fell short. You send his point, in his words, to the team drafting the next solicitation. A month later you tell him they are considering a capacity-building option and a shorter first-stage application. Nothing is decided yet, and you say that too.

feedback.text: You treated his correction as information, not an attack, and you were honest about both the scores and the limits of what you can change. Carrying his words forward, then reporting back, is what made his time count.
Keep the report-back specific: what was heard, who has it, what is being considered and when he will hear again.

choices.text: Explain that every applicant was held to the same criteria and the same scoring, walk through his scores, and assure him the process was fair to everyone.
choices.consequence: The director says he understands the rules were the same. That was his point. The call ends politely. His comment goes nowhere, and the next solicitation keeps the same capacity section.

feedback.text: Same criteria and equal access are different questions, like a correct address and a findable entrance. He was not saying the rules were applied unevenly. He was saying they favor one kind of organization.
Defending a process you worked hard on is a natural reaction. The readings ask you to take the particular correction seriously before defending the intention behind it.
What would you need to hear from applicants to know whether the capacity section measures what it is meant to?

choices.text: Tell him you agree, and promise that the next round will score community trust, so organizations like his that families rely on will have a fair chance.
choices.consequence: The director sounds hopeful. The next solicitation is drafted by another team under its own requirements, and community trust is not added as a criterion. When it is posted, he writes to ask what happened to your promise.

feedback.text: You heard him, which matters. The promise was not yours to make. The stronger choice carries his point to the people drafting the next round and tells him honestly what they will consider.
From the director’s side, a broken promise from the state may weigh more than the original disappointment.

choices.text: Listen closely without arguing, thank him for the feedback, explain his scores, and note “applicant disappointed with outcome” in the file so the record shows the call took place.
choices.consequence: The director feels heard on the call. The file now says he was disappointed, not what he said about grant writers and trust. Nobody drafting the next solicitation sees his point.

feedback.text: Listening without a route for the concern leaves the barrier where it was. Compare “disappointed with outcome” with “says the capacity section favors organizations that can pay grant writers.” One describes his feelings; the other carries his knowledge.
When you write up a debrief, record the specific point the applicant made in their words, and where you sent it.

decisions.setup: The director writes back: “So organizations like ours shouldn’t bother.” The question period still has ten days.
decisions.prompt: What do you do now?

choices.text: Tell him it is a fair question, find out which requirements are fixed for this grant, and post the answer for all applicants by a set date.
choices.consequence: You take the question to the person responsible for grants policy. The addendum goes out with a shorter narrative and a second way to submit. The director decides to apply.

feedback.text: You let his frustration point you back to the real question and gave him a date. That turns a closed answer into an open one.
His message was not giving up. It was a last check on whether the program meant what it said about reaching groups like his.

choices.text: Forward his email to your supervisor with a note that the requirements may need checking, and wait to hear back before replying, so you do not promise anything you cannot keep.
choices.consequence: Your supervisor agrees the requirements should be checked, and an addendum goes out a week later. The director heard nothing in between and nearly gave up. He applies, with less time to prepare.

feedback.text: Raising it was right. A short reply to the director saying what you were checking, and when he would hear, would have kept him in the process.
When you route a question, tell the person who asked: who has it and when they can expect an answer.

choices.text: Reply politely with the solicitation attached again, the date questions close, and a note that the requirements are explained in the attachment for every applicant.
choices.consequence: The director replies with one line: they will try, but meeting the audit and the page count means pulling staff from families for weeks. His proposal arrives on the last day, thinner than it could have been.

feedback.text: Resending the document answers a question he did not ask. His question was whether the requirements fit; only a check can answer that.
Which requirement in your current solicitation have you never checked the source of?

decisions.setup: The scores for Proposal 14 are far apart, and the comments explain them with tone and with beliefs about a community rather than with the proposal. The panel has not been dismissed.
decisions.prompt: What do you do before scores are final?

choices.text: Following the panel process, ask the reviewers to return to Proposal 14 and tie each comment to a criterion and to what the proposal says.
choices.consequence: The first reviewer rewrites his comment to name a capacity question. The second reviewer replaces her community statement with a line from the proposal’s own data. The scores move closer and the file can be explained to the applicant.

feedback.text: You used the process to correct the review instead of working around it. Every comment now points to evidence the applicant could see.
At the start of the next panel, say once: comments should point to a criterion and a page in the proposal.

choices.text: Flag the comments to your supervisor in writing, with the criteria they do not match, and let scoring proceed so the panel can finish on time today.
choices.consequence: Your supervisor notes the concern for next time. This round’s scores stand with the comments as written.

feedback.text: Raising the concern helps the next review. The panel was still in session, though, and the comments could have been tied to the criteria now.
What stopped you from raising it with the panel directly?

choices.text: Average the two scores and move on. Far-apart scores happen on every panel, and averaging settles them without favoring either reviewer.
choices.consequence: The average puts Proposal 14 just below the funding line. Its file explains the score with “unprofessional tone” and a statement about a community.

feedback.text: If the applicant asks why they were not funded, those comments are what they will read.
Spread in scores is normal. Comments that rest on style or on beliefs about a group are a different problem, and averaging does not fix it.

practiced: Separating a real requirement from a habit carried over from an older solicitation
Answering an applicant’s question through the person or area responsible, and for every applicant
Bringing a review panel back to the published criteria and to the applicant’s own words
Treating a favorable belief about a community as a shortcut, the same as an unfavorable one
Taking an applicant’s correction seriously before defending the process
Carrying an applicant’s point forward and telling them what happened to it
this_week: Pick one requirement in a solicitation or contract you manage and find out where it comes from.
Before your next review panel, write one sentence asking reviewers to tie each comment to a criterion and a page.
After your next debrief, send the applicant’s main point, in their words, to whoever drafts the next round.

simulations.intro: If you license, investigate or audit, your notes outlast the visit and shape how the next person reads a provider. In this version you run a licensing review, write the record, and hold an exit interview. Keep the standard clear, and keep your own reading of the person out of the record.
simulations.title: A licensing visit and the record that follows it
simulations.learner_role: You are a licensor in the Inspector General’s licensing area. You visit licensed programs, interview providers, review records against the standards, and write correction orders. Your notes and orders are read by other licensors, by investigators, and sometimes by the public.
simulations.background: Today you have a licensing review at a small licensed program that the provider has owned and run for eleven years. She supports a few adults with disabilities, and her last two reviews found no violations. When you scheduled the visit by phone, she asked whether an interpreter could join for the exit interview. On your team, your supervisor reviews correction orders before they go out. Voice note for recording: the provider speaks with a natural, confident delivery and no performed accent. She is competent and precise.

decisions.setup: The provider greets you in English. The walkthrough goes easily, and she answers your questions about the program. The interpreter you asked for was never booked. The scheduler’s note says, “Provider speaks English fine.” Next come the record review and the exit interview, where you will explain any violations and what she must do.
decisions.prompt: The provider asked for an interpreter for the exit interview. None is booked, and she seems at ease in English. What do you do?

choices.text: Go by her request, not the small talk. Ask what she needs for the exit interview, and bring in a qualified phone interpreter or set another time for that part.
choices.consequence: You say, “You asked for an interpreter for this part. I want to make sure you have one. Would a phone interpreter work, or would you rather finish on another day?” The provider says a phone interpreter is fine. She explains that everyday English is easy for her, but rules and orders are where she wants to be sure. The interpreter joins in twenty minutes, and you use the wait to start the record review. When you later explain a records issue, she asks two precise questions.

feedback.text: You trusted what she told you over what you heard in small talk. Asking what she needed, and arranging qualified help, kept her able to understand and answer the parts with real stakes. Build on it by telling the scheduler how the booking note missed her request.
For the provider, conversational English and the language of a correction order are different things. She knew that ahead of time and said so.
When someone tells you what they need, what makes you second-guess it?

choices.text: Proceed in English. She has handled every question easily so far, and setting another time would delay her license. You can speak slowly and check that she follows.
choices.consequence: You begin the record review in English. The provider answers in short phrases and nods often. When you start explaining the medication standard, you are not sure she is following, and she does not ask questions. Whatever you write next, she may not fully understand what it will ask of her.

feedback.text: It is easy to judge someone’s language needs by how a casual conversation goes. But she asked ahead of time, for the part where rules and stakes come in. Her request is the evidence.
Compare this with asking what she needs and arranging a phone interpreter. That costs twenty minutes. It protects her ability to understand an order she is responsible for meeting.

choices.text: Ask the provider’s adult daughter, who is visiting and offers to help, to interpret for the exit interview. Her mother trusts her, and no one has to wait for a phone line.
choices.consequence: The provider’s daughter agrees. She translates quickly, sometimes summing up. When you explain the medication standard, mother and daughter talk for a while, and the provider’s daughter says, “She understands.” You do not know what was said. The provider’s daughter is family, not a qualified interpreter, and this is the part of the visit where the provider learns what she must fix.

feedback.text: Using family is quick and can feel natural. But good intentions do not make someone a qualified interpreter, and you cannot check what was conveyed. A qualified interpreter protects the provider and the accuracy of your visit.
For the provider’s daughter, carrying a regulatory conversation about her mother’s license is a lot to ask. For the provider, it may change what she feels able to ask in front of her daughter.

choices.text: Ask the provider, kindly, why she wants an interpreter when her English sounds so good, so you can decide whether it is worth delaying the exit interview.
choices.consequence: The provider’s face tightens. “The rules and the order,” she says. “That is where I want to be sure. I asked for this when you scheduled.” The question made her defend a reasonable request. She agrees to go on in English so she does not seem difficult. The visit continues with less trust than it started with.

feedback.text: The question may come from real surprise. But it asks her to justify a need she already named, and puts her in the position of proving it.
Ask about the task instead: “What would help you most for the exit interview?”

decisions.setup: In the record review, two weeks of medication entries for one resident are not in the medication record you expected to see. The provider says the entries are in a notebook her pharmacy gave her, which she has used for years. She brings it. The entries are there. One dose has no initials, and three entries do not show the time the dose was given. Whether the notebook itself can serve as the required record is a question for the current standard. The missing initials and times are not. Your draft visit note reads, “Provider was evasive about medication records and resistant to licensing requirements.”
decisions.prompt: Some entries are missing required details. Your draft note describes the provider’s attitude. What goes in the note?

choices.text: Write only what you saw: the pharmacy notebook, one dose without initials, three without times. Cite that, and ask the person or area responsible whether the notebook can serve as the record.
choices.consequence: Your note now reads: “Medication entries for two weeks were kept in a pharmacy-supplied notebook. One dose on the 14th had no initials. Three entries did not show the time given.” The correction order cites the missing initials and times. You email the person or area responsible for the medication standard to ask whether the notebook can serve as the required record. Your supervisor reviews the note and the order and has no questions. A licensor who visits in two years will see what happened, not your read of the provider’s attitude.

feedback.text: You cited what is clearly required and wrote only what you saw. “One dose had no initials” is an observation. “Evasive” adds a reason she never gave. Asking whether the notebook can count, instead of deciding it yourself, keeps a real requirement apart from a habit. Build on it by reading your notes the way the next licensor will.
To the next licensor, or an investigator, a word like “resistant” becomes the starting point. The provider would carry it into every future visit.
Which words in your recent notes describe what happened, and which describe what you thought it meant?

choices.text: Keep the note as drafted. The entries were not where you expected, the record has real gaps, and your professional judgment of how a provider responds is part of what a visit note records.
choices.consequence: You send the note and the correction order to your supervisor. The order is accurate. But the first thing anyone will read in the provider’s file is that she was evasive and resistant. An investigator looking at an unrelated complaint later would start from that frame. The provider, who brought the notebook as soon as you asked, would never see why her file reads that way.

feedback.text: After a hard review, a quick summary of how it felt is natural. But the record outlasts the feeling. Words like “evasive” add a motive you did not observe.
Compare “evasive” with “one dose had no initials; three entries did not show the time given.” The second holds the same violation and tells the next reader only what is known.

choices.text: Do not cite it. She has kept these entries faithfully for years in the pharmacy notebook, and the missing initials and times look like small gaps in an otherwise careful record.
choices.consequence: The provider is relieved. But the standard exists so every dose can be traced, and some of these doses cannot be fully traced. You send your draft note, still containing “evasive,” to your supervisor with no correction order. Respect for her experience did not change what the standard requires, and the note still describes her attitude.

feedback.text: You were trying to respect her experience, and that matters. But you can reconsider an assumption while keeping necessary standards clear. The stronger move cites the missing initials and times plainly, with no words about her attitude, and checks the notebook question with the person or area responsible.
For the residents in the provider’s care, a complete medication record is a safety protection. Leaving the gap unaddressed does not serve them, or her.

choices.text: Before you write anything, ask the provider about her cultural background, so the note can explain why she keeps her medication records differently from other providers.
choices.consequence: The provider looks puzzled. “The pharmacy gave me the notebook,” she says. “It is easier.” The question had nothing to do with the record, and it suggested her background was the problem. You send your supervisor the draft note as it was, with the order.

feedback.text: Wanting to understand the reason for a practice is reasonable. But curiosity needs a purpose tied to the task. Her answer, that it was easier, was there to hear by asking about the notebook.
Try: “Can you show me how you have been using this notebook?” That asks about the practice, not about her.

decisions.setup: Your supervisor calls you before the exit interview. “The missing initials and times are a clear violation. They need to be cited. And this note says ‘evasive.’ What did she do that was evasive?” You think back. She brought the notebook as soon as you asked.
decisions.prompt: Your supervisor has asked you to back up a word in your record. What do you do?

choices.text: Tell your supervisor what you actually saw. Rewrite the note to describe what happened, cite the missing initials and times, and check whether the same word went anywhere else.
choices.consequence: You say, “She did not hide anything. I wrote what it felt like, not what happened.” You rewrite the note: the pharmacy notebook, the missing initials, the missing times. You find “resistant” also appears in your visit notes in the case system, and you fix that too. You ask the person or area responsible whether the notebook can serve as the required record. Your supervisor clears the correction order. The record now says what happened.

feedback.text: You took the question as a chance to check your account, not defend it. Following the word into the case system shows that a private change of mind is not enough when the old account has traveled. Next, notice what made that word come so easily.
For your supervisor, clearing an order means standing behind it. A note he can defend with facts protects him, you, and the provider.

choices.text: Tell your supervisor it is a judgment call. You were in the room and he was not, and a licensor’s read of a visit is part of the record for a reason.
choices.consequence: Your supervisor asks you to name the facts. You struggle to find any. He asks you to remove the word and cite the violation, and he clears the order once you do. The note changes, but only because he insisted. The habit that produced the word is untouched.

feedback.text: Standing by a judgment you cannot support with an observation is different from professional confidence. A stronger answer says what you saw.
When someone asks you to back up a word, how do you tell a judgment from an impression?

choices.text: Agree the word is strong. Change “evasive” to “reluctant,” which is gentler and closer to how the review felt, cite the violation, and send the note back to him.
choices.consequence: Your supervisor reads the new word and sighs. “Reluctant” still describes her attitude, not what happened. She brought the notebook as soon as you asked. The note comes back to you a second time, and the exit interview starts late.

feedback.text: A softer word still adds a motive she did not give. The fix is not a gentler label. It is no label, just the observation.
Try writing the sentence a camera could have captured: what was in the notebook, which dose lacked initials, and which entries lacked times.

decisions.setup: At the exit interview, you explain the correction order: every dose must be initialed and show the time given. The provider listens, then says, “In the review you said I did not keep the record. I kept every entry. They are in the other book. Eleven years, and no problems. You make me sound careless.” She is upset. The violation is real. Her account of what she did is also real. Whether an interpreter is on the line depends on what you arranged earlier. This is the part the provider asked for help with.
decisions.prompt: The provider has corrected how you described her. The violation still stands. How do you respond?

choices.text: Name the specific thing you got wrong: she kept every entry. Keep the order. Explain what it asks, what she can choose, and how she can request a review.
choices.consequence: You say, “You are right. You kept every entry. I said you did not keep the record, and that was not accurate. The order is about the missing initials and times.” You tell her you will find out whether the notebook can serve as the required record, and let her know. She asks whether the order goes in her file. You say yes, and explain how she can request a review if she disagrees, and whom to contact. If no interpreter has joined, you offer to set a short follow-up call with one, so she can ask about the order in the language she chose. You ask what would make initials and times easier to record. She says she will initial and time each dose as she gives it. She is still unhappy about the order. She also says, “Thank you for saying that.”

feedback.text: You named the specific inaccuracy without asking her to make you feel better, and you did not give up the standard to smooth things over. Explaining her review route, in a language she can use, respects her rights in the process. Build on it by bringing her the answer about the notebook, and checking at follow-up that each dose is initialed and timed.
For the provider, eleven years of care is part of who she is as a provider. Hearing you correct the specific word matters, even with the order in place.
When a provider corrects your account, how do you keep the correction and the standard both in view?

choices.text: Explain calmly that the order is not personal. You are doing your job, the standard applies to every provider the same way, and her long history is not in question here.
choices.consequence: The provider says, “I know it applies to everyone. I am saying what you said about me was not true.” You repeat that it is not personal. She says nothing more and signs where you show her. The order is accurate. Her correction was never answered.

feedback.text: The standard does apply to everyone, and saying so is true. But she was correcting a specific description, not disputing the rule. Answering the rule instead of the correction leaves her point unheard.
Under pushback, “it is not personal” can feel calming. Here it skips the part that was personal: a word about her.

choices.text: Withdraw the correction order. Her eleven-year record is strong, the gaps are small, and repairing the relationship now will do more for the residents than a citation will.
choices.consequence: The provider is relieved. Your supervisor is not. He reminds you that one dose has no initials and three entries have no times. The order is reissued the next week, now with a note that it was withdrawn and issued again. The provider is more confused than before, and the repair you meant to offer has become a second surprise.

feedback.text: Wanting to make things right with a provider who feels judged is understandable. But the standard and her feelings are separate. You can correct an inaccurate word without dropping a real violation.
A stronger response corrects your description and keeps the order. That repairs what was inaccurate without creating a new problem.

choices.text: Apologize warmly and at length for any offense you caused, tell her how much her work matters, and ask whether she can forgive you before you leave today.
choices.consequence: The provider says it is fine, because you seem to need her to say so. The conversation is now about how you feel. She still does not know what you got wrong, or how to ask for a review of the order. You leave with her reassurance and without giving her the answer she needed.

feedback.text: A broad apology that asks for forgiveness puts the work of repair on her. Naming the specific inaccuracy gives her less to manage and more to rely on.
Try: “You kept every entry. I said you did not, and that was not accurate. Here is what the order asks, and here is how you can ask for a review.”

practiced: Going by a person’s stated communication need, and arranging qualified help
Writing what you observed instead of a motive you inferred
Citing what a standard clearly requires, and checking a format question with the person or area responsible
Holding a clear standard while reconsidering your read of the person
Asking about a practice, not about a person’s background
Following an inaccurate word to everywhere it went in the record
Correcting your description of a provider without giving up a real violation
this_week: Reread your last three visit notes. Mark any word that describes a provider’s attitude, and ask what you actually saw.
Check how interpreter requests made at scheduling reach you before a visit, and who to tell when one is missed.
Before your next exit interview, write one sentence that states the violation plainly and one that explains how the provider can ask for a review.
When a provider corrects you this week, try naming the specific thing you got wrong before you explain anything else.

simulations.intro: If you run a program, a plan crosses your desk long before anyone feels its effects. In this version you turn a new law into a notice, weigh two supervisors’ views on one budget, and report on how the launch went. Watch the difference between an arrangement on paper and help that people can actually use.
simulations.title: Turning a new law into a notice people can use
simulations.learner_role: You are a Human Services Manager. You run a statewide program and supervise three supervisors. You turn legislative requirements into services, decide how staff time and budget are used, and sign off on implementation plans.
simulations.background: The legislature changed your program. In six months, everyone enrolled must get a reassessment notice 60 days before their eligibility review, and the notice must explain how to ask for help. You have a fixed amount of new money. Your implementation plan is due to your division director in three weeks. Three supervisors report to you: the call-line supervisor; the notices supervisor, who leads notices and policy; and the county relations supervisor, who works with counties and lead agencies. The plan includes an equity analysis and a language-access checklist.

decisions.setup: In the plan review, the notices supervisor walks through the checklist. Next to “People are informed about interpreter services,” the box is checked. The note says, “Interpreter contract in place.” The call-line supervisor frowns. Call-line staff hear from people who did not know they could ask for an interpreter, he says, and some calls end before the person reaches one. The notices supervisor says the contract covers every language the program sees. Both are describing something real.
decisions.prompt: The checklist says met. Your call-line supervisor says people cannot use it. What do you do with that line before you sign the plan?

choices.text: Leave the box checked. The contract covers every language the program sees, which meets the requirement, and the call-line issue is a training question for the call-line team to handle.
choices.consequence: The plan is on track to reach your director on time. The call-line supervisor tells his staff to remind callers about interpreter help. The notice still says nothing about it. The notices supervisor moves on to the next line. The call-line supervisor says little for the rest of the review. He came with a real pattern from the phones, and it was filed as his team’s problem.

feedback.text: Contracts and checklists feel solid, and deadlines push toward signing. But a contract shows an arrangement, not that people can get the help. The checklist was asking a question the contract does not answer.
Compare this with keeping the contract information and asking how requests work in practice. That takes a week. It finds the gap before launch, not after.

choices.text: Keep the contract details, but mark the line not yet supported. Ask the call-line and notices supervisors how a request works on a real call, and name who checks by when.
choices.consequence: The notices supervisor is a little stung, then interested. The contract is real; no one had asked her how it works on the phones. The call-line supervisor pulls two weeks of call notes. They show that the current notice never mentions interpreter help, and that staff transfer callers to the interpreter line without explaining the wait. The county relations supervisor adds that counties field the same confusion. The plan now has a named gap, an owner and a date, instead of a checked box.

feedback.text: You kept what is known, the contract, while making the evidence gap visible. That is what a checklist is for: pointing to questions, not settling them. Build on it by asking people who call the line how the help worked for them.
For the notices supervisor, being told her line was wrong would have felt like blame. Being asked how it works in practice let her help find the answer.
Which checked boxes in your current plans rest on an arrangement, and which rest on evidence that people can use it?

choices.text: Drop the checklist from the plan. If a checked box cannot show whether people actually get help, it is not worth the time, and cutting it frees time for the work that matters.
choices.consequence: The notices supervisor removes the checklist. The plan is shorter. The call-line supervisor’s concern is still there, but now nothing in the plan asks about language access at all. The question that might have led your team to the notice wording leaves with the form.

feedback.text: You saw the limit of a checked box, which is real. The stronger move keeps the tool and asks for the evidence behind it. A checklist can still point to a useful question.
Next time, ask: “What would show that this line is true for the people calling?” Keep the line open until someone can answer.

choices.text: Act on the call-line concern now. Direct the notices supervisor to translate the notice into ten more languages and add a second interpreter vendor before launch, without waiting for more information.
choices.consequence: The notices supervisor starts the translation work, which would use most of the new money. The call-line supervisor points out that what his staff hear most is not about the notice language. Callers do not know they can ask for an interpreter, and transfers end without explanation. The money is close to committed before anyone has checked what the barrier is.

feedback.text: Acting fast on an access concern comes from a good place. But a change made before the concern is examined can miss what people actually face.
A stronger move asks the call-line supervisor what the call notes show first. The evidence may support translation, or something closer to the barrier and less costly.

decisions.setup: Now the budget. The new money covers one of two options. Option one adds call-line staff for the months around review dates. Option two rewrites the notice in plain language, adds a line about free interpreter help, and tests the draft with people who receive it. The notices supervisor would add one line about interpreter help and keep the rest of the notice. “The same words for everyone is fair,” she says. “Consistency protects people.” The call-line supervisor wants staff. The law requires certain content and the 60-day timing. It does not require the current wording.
decisions.prompt: Your supervisors disagree, and the money covers one option. How do you make the call?

choices.text: Separate what the law requires from habit. Honor the notices supervisor’s value of consistency, ask whether the same words give people the same chance to act, and say how you will decide.
choices.consequence: You list the legal requirements on the whiteboard: certain content, 60-day timing, how to ask for help. Everything else is open. You tell the notices supervisor that consistency matters, and ask whether the current wording, full of terms only staff use, gives people an equal chance to act. She looks at the call notes and says, “Probably not.” The county relations supervisor suggests testing a draft with county workers and a few people who get the notice. You choose the rewrite, keep a small amount for peak staffing, and explain your reasons to both supervisors. The call-line supervisor is disappointed. He also knows his evidence shaped the choice.

feedback.text: You separated a real requirement from an avoidable habit, and you treated the notices supervisor’s value as worth keeping, not wrong. That let her reconsider without losing face. Build on it by telling the team how the test results could change the plan.
To the notices supervisor, consistency is a way to protect people from unfair treatment. Asking whether equal wording gives equal access respects that value and widens it.
Which parts of your program’s routines are required, and which are habits that feel required because they are familiar?

choices.text: Choose the notice rewrite now. The call notes already point clearly to the notice, so there is no need to reopen the debate with the notices supervisor or spend another meeting on it.
choices.consequence: The rewrite is funded. The notices supervisor carries it out, but she still believes the old wording was fairer, and she drops the test with readers to save time. The new notice reads better to staff. No one knows yet whether it reads better to the people who get it.

feedback.text: The evidence did point to the notice. Skipping the notices supervisor’s value left her carrying out a change she did not believe in, and the test that would show the effect fell away.

To the notices supervisor, consistency is a way to protect people from unfair treatment. Being skipped told her that value did not count, so she had little reason to protect the parts of the plan she did not choose.
When the evidence seems to settle a choice, whose reasons do you still need to hear before you decide?

choices.text: Go with the notices supervisor’s view. She leads notices and policy, the notice is her area, and she knows the wording rules better than anyone else at the table.
choices.consequence: The notices supervisor adds the interpreter line and keeps the rest of the notice as is, and the money goes to call-line staff. The call-line supervisor notices how the choice was made: the call notes about confusing terms never came up. He takes it as a sign that call-line knowledge does not count in policy choices. In his next staff meeting, he stops raising caller patterns. The disagreement is settled, and an important source of knowledge goes quiet.

feedback.text: To the call-line supervisor, deferring to the policy lead says that role decides whose knowledge counts. If only expert accounts count, barriers that front-line staff see can stay outside decisions.
Relying on the person whose area it is can feel like good delegation. It works best when that person’s view has been tested against what others know.

choices.text: Split the money evenly between the two options, so neither supervisor feels overruled and both of their concerns get at least some of the new funding this year.
choices.consequence: Each supervisor gets half. Half is not enough to staff the peak months or to test a new notice. The notices supervisor makes small wording edits without testing them. The call-line supervisor adds one part-time worker. Neither change is big enough to tell whether it helped. The decision avoided the conflict, and the access question with it.

feedback.text: Splitting the difference avoids choosing, but it also avoids asking which option meets the barrier. A clear decision with stated reasons respects both supervisors more than a split that serves neither.
Next time, try: “Here is what the law requires. Here is what the evidence shows. Here is my decision and why. Tell me what I might be missing.”

decisions.setup: After the meeting, the call-line supervisor stops by with a printout of call notes. One reads: “Caller asked if someone could explain the letter in her language. Did not know to ask for an interpreter. Transfer dropped.” Another: “Caller’s son interpreted. Unsure of review date.” He says, “This is what the box doesn’t show.”
decisions.prompt: You have the plan in front of you and new information from the call line. What do you do now?

choices.text: Reopen the language-access line. Ask the call-line and notices supervisors to trace one call together, from notice to interpreter, and name who checks the fix by when.
choices.consequence: The two supervisors spend an afternoon walking through a single call. They find that the notice says nothing about free interpreter help, and that transfers have no warm handoff. They also flag the call where a caller’s son interpreted: if the notice and the call line made interpreter help clear, no one would need to rely on family for a review date. The plan now names two fixes, who owns each, and a date to check whether callers reach help. The box stays unchecked until then.

feedback.text: You let a concrete account change a plan you had settled. Tracing one real path is often faster than debating the whole system. Next, decide how you will hear from callers after the change.
For the call-line supervisor, bringing the notes was a risk. Seeing them change the plan tells him it was worth it.

choices.text: Thank the call-line supervisor for the notes and add a line to the plan: “Call-line staff report some confusion; monitor after launch.” That records the concern without holding up the deadline.
choices.consequence: The line is accurate and asks nothing of anyone. No one owns the monitoring, and no date is set. The call-line supervisor files the printout. The dropped transfers will keep happening after launch, now with a note in the plan saying the agency knew.

feedback.text: A note that names a concern without an owner or a date hears it without acting on it. Naming who will check, what, and when turns it into follow-through.
Try asking both supervisors: “Can the two of you own this? What would you need to check it by the end of next month?”

choices.text: Ask the call-line supervisor which caller groups seem most confused, so the plan can target outreach and translated materials to those communities and make the most of a tight budget.
choices.consequence: The call-line supervisor hesitates. The notes show individual callers who did not know they could ask for help. They do not show that a group is confused. A fix built on a guess about which communities struggle would miss the people the guess leaves out, and it would not touch the notice or the transfers.

feedback.text: Wanting to target effort makes sense with a tight budget. But a few individual accounts do not make a group profile. These notes point to a process problem: the notice and the transfer.
When you hear a few accounts, how quickly do you turn them into a statement about a group?

decisions.setup: Four months after launch, your director asks for an update. The notices supervisor’s draft report says, “No complaints received. Notice rollout successful.” The same week, the county relations supervisor forwards an email from a county eligibility supervisor. Her workers still get calls from people who do not understand what the notice asks them to do. She writes, “Maybe it’s just our county.”
decisions.prompt: The report says success. A county partner says otherwise. What goes to your director?

choices.text: Report what was done and what is still unknown. Ask the county eligibility supervisor what her workers hear, ask for call-line patterns, and say when she will hear back.
choices.consequence: Your update says the notice went out on time, no formal complaints were filed, and early county reports suggest some people still do not understand the next step. It names a check: the call-line team will sample calls, and the county relations supervisor will ask three counties what workers hear. Results go to your director in six weeks. You call the county eligibility supervisor yourself. She says it helps to be asked directly. Her answer points to one confusing sentence about where to send forms.

feedback.text: You kept what was done, what was heard, and what is still unknown as separate claims. No complaints is missing information, not proof. Calling the county eligibility supervisor closed the loop with the person who raised it. Build on it by telling her what changed because of her email.
For the county eligibility supervisor, “Maybe it’s just our county” was a way to raise a concern without seeming to complain. Your call told her a county account counts as evidence.
In updates to your director, try three parts: “Here is what was done. Here is what is known about the effect. Here is how and when the agency will learn more.”

choices.text: Send the notices supervisor’s report. No complaints after four months is a good sign, the notice went out on time, and one county’s email is not enough to change the story.
choices.consequence: Your director shares the report upward. The county eligibility supervisor does not hear back. Three months later, completed reviews drop in several counties, and staff trace it to the same unclear sentence about where to send forms. The report that said success is the record leaders relied on.

feedback.text: It is natural to trust a clean report after a hard launch. But no feedback does not show a barrier is gone. People who struggle with a notice often do not file complaints.
Compare this with reporting what is known and what is not, and asking the county eligibility supervisor what she sees. One county is not proof of a statewide problem. It is a reason to look.

choices.text: Add the county email to the report as an exception, so the county concern is on record, and keep the overall finding of success that the lack of complaints supports.
choices.consequence: The report now says success, with one county reporting issues. Your director reads it as a local problem. The county eligibility supervisor gets a thank-you email from the county relations supervisor. No one checks whether other counties see the same thing, so the confusing sentence stays in the notice.

feedback.text: Naming the county concern was better than leaving it out. Labeling it an exception decides what it means before anyone checks. A stronger update keeps the effect open and says how you will find out.
When one partner raises a problem, how do you decide whether it is local or a sign of something wider?

choices.text: Ask the county eligibility supervisor to survey her workers and the people they serve, and send you a full analysis before you report anything, so the update rests on real evidence.
choices.consequence: The county eligibility supervisor’s team is already stretched. She replies that she cannot run a survey for a state program. Your update to the director slips. The county’s knowledge reached you, and the request to do the agency’s analysis pushed it back out.

feedback.text: Wanting solid evidence before you report is responsible. But asking a partner to do your team’s analysis shifts staff work onto them.
Ask her one focused question, such as: “What do workers hear most often about the notice?” Then have your own team do the checking.

practiced: Treating a checked box as a question that needs evidence, not as proof of access
Telling an arrangement, like an interpreter contract, apart from whether people can use it
Separating what a law requires from habits that grew around it
Asking whether the same words give people the same chance to act
Weighing front-line and county knowledge alongside policy expertise
Reporting what was done, what is known, and what is still unknown
this_week: Pick one checked line in a current plan. Write down the evidence behind it, and what would show it holds for the people it is meant to reach.
Ask a call-line or county partner one focused question about a notice or process your program runs: what do people find hardest to use?
In your next budget or staffing choice, list what the law requires and what is habit before you compare options.
Look at your most recent status report. Does any line treat “no complaints” as proof that something works?

simulations.intro: If you write policy or guidance, your words become what staff do in thousands of meetings you will never see. In this version you draft a bulletin with a workgroup that includes a self-advocate who uses services. Watch for the moment when background information starts to answer a question only the person can answer.

cast.label: the advocate from a listed community
the advocate who asked for plain language

simulations.title: A bulletin about who is in the room
simulations.learner_role: You are a Human Services Program Consultant. You draft policy bulletins and guidance for county and lead-agency case managers, lead a workgroup of partners, and carry the equity analysis for your drafts. Your words become the instructions case managers follow in thousands of planning meetings.
simulations.background: Your team is writing a bulletin for case managers about support planning meetings for people with disabilities. It tells case managers how to ask whom the person wants at their meeting, and how to document that choice. Person-centered practice and informed choice are at its center. A workgroup reviews your drafts: county and lead-agency staff, two advocates, and a self-advocate who uses services. You send drafts to the workgroup in the format each member asked for, the self-advocate included. Your lead wants the bulletin out before the next planning cycle, six weeks away. The documentation fields live in a statewide system, and changing a field label takes months.

decisions.setup: At the second workgroup meeting, the county lead suggests adding a section called “Cultural considerations.” It would list which communities tend to prefer family-led decisions, so case managers know when to invite family. She has a fact sheet ready. Others nod. It would be quick to add. You notice it would tell case managers what to expect from a person before they ask.
decisions.prompt: The county lead’s idea comes from care and would be easy to add. What do you do with it in the bulletin?

choices.text: Thank the county lead, and use the knowledge to shape questions, not answers. Draft guidance that has case managers ask each person whom they want involved and what would help.
choices.consequence: You say, “This could help case managers prepare. I want to use it so they ask better questions, not so they assume the answer.” The county lead is unsure at first, then helps rewrite. The new section says family can matter a great deal to many people, and a person may still want one conversation alone. It gives case managers sample questions: “Who would you like at your meeting?” and “Is there anything you would like to talk about privately?” The self-advocate says it is the first draft that sounds written for him.

feedback.text: You kept the county lead’s knowledge and changed its job, from predicting to preparing. At bulletin scale, that choice reaches every planning meeting. Build on it by checking that the documentation guidance records what the person said, not a group expectation.
For the county lead, the fact sheet was a way to help case managers do right by families. Rewriting it with her, rather than cutting it, kept her in the work.
Where in your own guidance does background information tell staff what to expect, instead of what to ask?

choices.text: Add the section as the county lead proposed. Case managers keep asking for practical guidance, the fact sheet is well sourced, and it would help them know when to invite family.
choices.consequence: The section goes into the draft. The self-advocate reads it during the meeting and goes quiet. A general statement in a state bulletin is about to become a default in thousands of meetings, and no one has said so out loud.

feedback.text: Practical, sourced guidance is what case managers ask for, so this is an easy yes. But a fact sheet about a group cannot tell you what one person wants. At bulletin scale, it becomes the expectation.
Compare this with using the same knowledge to write better questions. Case managers still get practical help, and the person still decides.

choices.text: Thank the county lead, but remove all mention of culture and family from the bulletin, so no case manager can read any part of it as stereotyping the people they serve.
choices.consequence: The draft is neutral and thin. The county lead feels her contribution was rejected. Case managers will still walk into meetings with their own assumptions about family, just without guidance on how to ask. The risk you wanted to avoid is still there, unaddressed.

feedback.text: Avoiding the subject keeps the bulletin from stereotyping, but it also leaves case managers without a way to ask. Knowledge used to prepare questions is different from knowledge used to predict.
When a topic feels risky, do you tend to cut it or reframe it? What does each cost?

choices.text: Ask the advocate from a listed community, the only workgroup member from one of those communities, to write the section, so it is accurate and draws on lived knowledge.
choices.consequence: The advocate from a listed community says she can share her own experience but cannot describe what a whole community prefers. She is an advocate with her own job, not a state policy writer. She agrees reluctantly, and the section is delayed. She tells another advocate she was invited for her knowledge, then handed the agency’s work because of who she is.

feedback.text: To the advocate from a listed community, this asked her to represent a community and do staff work at once. Her knowledge is valuable. It is not a population profile, and the writing is your job.
